a: When the first true leaves appear after the seed leaves
As soon as the seed is in the soil
When the plant has finished flowering
111962.e: The seed leaves often look different from the later leaves. When the first true leaves appear, the little plants are strong enough.
111962.m: You prick out as soon as the first true leaves appear.

111963.q: Which simple tool is often used for pricking out?
111963.e: With a dibber you lift seedlings out of the soil and make planting holes. A pencil or chopstick works too.
111963.m: A dibber helps when moving seedlings.

111964.q: The German gardening word “pikieren” (pricking out) comes from which language?
111964.e: It comes from the French verb “piquer”, which means “to prick”. When pricking out, you poke holes for the little plants.
111964.m: “Pikieren” comes from the French word for prick.

111965.q: Where is the best place to hold a seedling when pricking it out?
a: Not at all, you shake it out
111965.e: The thin stem bends easily and cannot grow back. A seed leaf copes better with a small injury.
111965.m: Hold seedlings by the leaf, not the stem.

111966.q: Why are seedlings that are too crowded pricked out?
a: Otherwise they would take light and space from each other
So that they grow in winter
Because otherwise they get too sweet
111966.e: In a crowded sowing, the little plants compete for light, water and nutrients. When separated, they grow stronger.

111967.q: Which soil is good for sowing and pricking out?
a: Fine seed compost low in nutrients
111967.e: Young plants need loose, fine soil. Few nutrients encourage the roots to grow strongly and search.
111967.m: For seedlings, use loose seed compost with few nutrients.

111968.q: What is meant by biological plant protection?
a: Fighting pests with natural enemies and remedies
111968.e: Biological plant protection relies on helpful creatures, plant extracts and preventive measures. Synthetic chemicals are avoided.
111968.m: Biological plant protection uses nature's helpers.

111969.q: What kind of living thing is Bacillus thuringiensis, which organic farmers use against leaf-eating caterpillars?
111969.e: Bacillus thuringiensis is a bacterium. It makes proteins that are poisonous to certain caterpillars but harmless to people and most other animals.
111969.m: A bacterium helps against hungry caterpillars.

111970.q: Which home-made plant brew is often used against aphids in organic gardens?
111970.e: Nettles are soaked in water and sprayed in diluted form. The brew is meant to drive away aphids and, as a fertiliser, makes the plants stronger.
111970.m: You can make a brew for the garden from nettles.

111971.q: What is a fine insect mesh over a vegetable bed for?
a: It keeps insects such as the cabbage root fly away
It warms the soil like a heater
111971.e: The fine mesh lets light, air and water through. But harmful flies and moths cannot lay their eggs on the plants.
111971.m: A protective mesh keeps harmful insects away physically.

111972.q: Which tiny worms can be added to watering water to fight vine weevil larvae?
111972.e: Certain nematodes (roundworms) get into the larvae and kill them. You buy them from specialist shops and water them in.
111972.m: Helpful nematodes fight beetle larvae in the soil.

111973.q: Which insects are released in greenhouses against whitefly?
111973.e: Parasitic wasps such as Encarsia formosa lay their eggs in whitefly larvae. This makes the larvae die.
111973.m: Parasitic wasps are little helpers against whitefly.

111974.q: What do pheromone traps in the garden use to attract harmful insects?
111974.e: Pheromones are scents that insects use to find each other. The insects that are lured in get stuck in the trap, for example codling moths.
111974.m: Pheromone traps attract insects with scents.

111975.q: Why is healthy, loose soil part of preventive plant protection?
a: Strong plants are less likely to suffer from pests
Because pests cannot see loose soil
111975.e: Well-fed plants grow strongly and can cope better with pests. Prevention is a basic principle of biological plant protection.
111975.m: Healthy plants grow in healthy soil.

111976.q: Which garden creature is known for eating lots of aphids, along with its larvae?
111976.e: Ladybirds, and especially their larvae, eat huge numbers of aphids. They are among the best-known helpful creatures in the garden.
111976.m: The ladybird is a busy aphid hunter.

111977.q: Which larva is called the “aphid lion” because of its appetite for aphids?
a: The caterpillar of the large white butterfly
111977.e: Lacewing larvae grab aphids with their sucking jaws. That is why they have the nickname aphid lion.
111977.m: Lacewing larvae are also called aphid lions.

111978.q: What shelter can you hang in a fruit tree for earwigs?
a: An upside-down flowerpot filled with wood wool
111978.e: During the day, earwigs like to hide in dry hollow spaces. At night they eat aphids, among other things.
111978.m: A pot of wood wool is a hotel for earwigs.

111979.q: Which mammal eats snails, beetles and worms in the garden and hibernates?
111979.e: Hedgehogs hunt insects, snails and other small animals at night. Piles of leaves and branches give them a place to hibernate.
111979.m: The hedgehog is a night-time helper in the garden.

111980.q: Why do people put an insect hotel in the garden?
a: As a nesting place for wild bees and other insects
To catch insects and sell them
As a feeding place for hedgehogs
111980.e: Wild bees in particular lay their eggs in the tubes and holes. Wild bees pollinate many flowers in the garden.
111980.m: An insect hotel gives wild bees a nursery.

111981.q: Which birds are especially helpful because they collect lots of caterpillars for their young?
111981.e: Tits feed their young mainly on insects and caterpillars. A nest box attracts them into the garden.

111982.q: Which flying insects look like small wasps but do not sting, and have larvae that eat aphids?
111982.e: Hoverflies disguise themselves with wasp colours but are harmless. Their larvae eat lots of aphids.

111983.q: Which snake-like animal likes to eat slugs in the garden but is not a snake at all?
111983.e: The slow worm looks like a snake but is a legless lizard. It is harmless and eats slugs and worms.
111983.m: The slow worm is a lizard without legs.

111984.q: Which slug is seen as a particularly annoying pest in Swiss gardens?
111984.e: The Spanish slug does not originally come from Switzerland but probably from western Europe, and it breeds a lot. It often eats young vegetable plants bare overnight.
111984.m: The Spanish slug eats lots of young plants.

111985.q: Which striped beetle eats the leaves of potato plants?
111985.e: The Colorado potato beetle comes from North America and was brought to Europe. It and its red larvae eat potato leaves.
111985.m: The Colorado potato beetle came to Europe from North America.

111986.q: Which sweet substance given off by aphids attracts ants?
111986.e: Aphids suck sugary plant sap and give off the extra as honeydew. Ants protect the aphids so they can collect it.
111986.m: Ants milk aphids for their honeydew.

111987.q: Whose caterpillars eat holes in cabbage leaves?
111987.e: The large white lays its eggs on cabbage plants. The green caterpillars can eat the leaves down to the veins.
111987.m: Large white caterpillars love eating cabbage leaves.

111988.q: Which moth, brought in from East Asia, eats box hedges bare?
111988.e: The box tree moth was brought to Europe and spread quickly. Its caterpillars eat box plants down to the wood.
111988.m: The box tree moth threatens many box hedges.

111989.q: Which rodent eats roots, tubers and flower bulbs underground in the garden?
111989.e: The vole feeds on plants and eats roots and tubers. The mole, on the other hand, eats animals such as earthworms.
111989.m: The vole eats roots, the mole eats worms.

111990.q: Which small fly, brought in from Asia, lays its eggs in ripe cherries and berries?
111990.e: The spotted wing drosophila pierces healthy, ripening fruit and lays eggs there. The fruit then turns mushy.
111990.m: The spotted wing drosophila attacks ripe berries and cherries.

111991.q: How do aphids suck up their food?
a: With a piercing mouthpart from the plant's sap channels
With tiny teeth from the roots
With their feet from the soil
With their wings from the air
111991.e: Aphids pierce the plant with their mouthpart and suck the sap. In doing so they can also spread virus diseases.
111991.m: Aphids suck plant sap with a beak-like mouthpart.

111992.q: Which two English words make up “permaculture”?
111992.e: The term comes from “permanent agriculture”, meaning long-lasting farming. The aim is systems that keep themselves going.

111993.q: In which country did Bill Mollison and David Holmgren develop permaculture in the 1970s?
111993.e: The two Australians published a first book on permaculture in 1978. Since then the idea has spread around the world.

111994.q: In permaculture, what decides how the garden is divided into zones?
a: How often you need to look after and visit an area
The alphabetical order of plant names
111994.e: Areas you use often, such as the herb bed, are close to the house. Areas that need little care, such as the wild area, are further away.
111994.m: In permaculture, the most important things are close to the house.

111995.q: Which idea is at the heart of permaculture?
a: Copying natural cycles and avoiding waste
Buying as much fertiliser as possible
Growing only one single kind of plant
111995.e: Permaculture takes ecosystems such as the forest as its model. Leftovers are used again, for example as compost or mulch.
111995.m: Permaculture copies the cycles of nature.

111996.q: What is a herb spiral, often found in permaculture gardens?
a: A spiral-shaped mound of stones with dry and damp spots
A herbal tea in a spiral shape
111996.e: At the top it is sunny and dry, at the bottom damp and cool. So herbs with different needs find a place in a small space.
111996.m: A herb spiral gives many herbs a place in a small space.

111997.q: Why is the soil covered with mulch in permaculture?
a: It protects against drying out and feeds soil creatures
So that the soil freezes faster
Because mulch turns the plants blue
111997.e: Mulch made of leaves, straw or grass cuttings keeps moisture in the soil. As it rots, it becomes food for soil creatures.
111997.m: Mulch keeps the soil moist and alive.

111998.q: What do you call a garden laid out like a forest in several layers, with trees, shrubs and herbs?
111998.e: A forest garden combines fruit trees, berry bushes, herbs and ground cover. Once it is set up, it needs little care.
111998.m: A forest garden grows in several layers.

111999.q: Why do people like to create a small pond in a permaculture garden?
a: It stores water and gives animals a habitat
So that you can swim in it
Because plants only grow in water
111999.e: A pond holds back rainwater and attracts frogs, dragonflies and birds. These help, for example, against slugs and pests.
111999.m: A pond stores water and brings life to the garden.

112000.q: Who is the German “Schrebergarten” (allotment garden) named after?
112000.e: Moritz Schreber campaigned for exercise in the fresh air. After his death, playgrounds and gardens in Leipzig were named after him.
112000.m: The Schrebergarten is named after a doctor from Leipzig.

112001.q: What are allotment gardens usually called in Switzerland?
112001.e: In Switzerland people usually speak of family gardens. They are often leased out by clubs on land owned by the municipality.
112001.m: In Switzerland, allotments are often called family gardens.

112002.q: What was the plan called with which Switzerland grew much more of its own food in the Second World War, even on sports fields and in parks?
112002.e: The Cultivation Battle (Anbauschlacht) is also called the Wahlen Plan after its creator, Friedrich Traugott Wahlen. At that time vegetables were also grown in many family gardens and allotments in the cities.
112002.m: In the Cultivation Battle, Switzerland planted vegetables and potatoes everywhere.

112003.q: Why did allotment gardens appear in the growing cities of the 19th century?
a: Working families were meant to have a place to relax and their own vegetables
112003.e: Cramped city flats lacked greenery. A small garden offered fresh air, exercise and extra food.
112003.m: Allotments brought greenery and vegetables into the cities.

112004.q: Who usually gives out an allotment garden?
a: A club that leases out the plots
112004.e: Allotments are usually organised in clubs. You lease a plot and must follow the garden rules.
112004.m: You usually lease an allotment from a club.

112005.q: What do you call a single piece of garden in an allotment site?
112005.e: An allotment site is divided into many plots. Each plot is leased by one person or family.
112005.m: An allotment is a plot on a garden site.

112006.q: What small hut for tools stands in many allotment gardens?
112006.e: The garden shed is used as a shelter and a store for tools. Living in it is usually not allowed.
112006.m: Garden tools are kept in the garden shed.

112007.q: What do many sets of rules for family gardens require?
a: That part of the area is used for vegetables, fruit or flowers
That the whole garden is concreted over
That a swimming pool is built every year
112007.e: Family gardens are meant for growing things, not just for leisure. That is why clubs often set rules on how the area is used.
112007.m: A family garden is mainly there for gardening.

112008.q: Which types of wood are especially good for the sides of a raised bed?
112008.e: Larch and Douglas fir wood contain lots of resin and resist damp for a long time. That is why they rot more slowly than other woods.
112008.m: Wood rich in resin lasts longer in a raised bed.

112009.q: Where should you put little plants that have just been pricked out?
a: Somewhere bright, but not in full sun
112009.e: After being moved, the roots first have to settle in again. Full sun would dry the little plants out during this time.
112009.m: Pricked-out plants need light but protection from full sun.

112010.q: Why should potatoes not grow straight after tomatoes in the same place?
a: Both are nightshades with the same diseases
Tomatoes make the soil too acidic for tubers
Tomato roots grow into the potatoes
112010.e: Potatoes and tomatoes belong to the same plant family. Diseases such as late blight attack both.
112010.m: Related vegetables should not follow each other in crop rotation.

112011.q: Which beetles, usually dark and shiny, hunt snails and insects on the ground at night?
112011.e: Ground beetles are quick hunters. Many species eat slug eggs, small slugs and insect larvae.
112011.m: Ground beetles are night-time hunters in the garden soil.

a: A paper strip with seeds at the right spacing
A rubber band for seed packets
112012.e: In seed tape, the seeds are already set at the right distances. You lay it in the seed drill and cover it with soil.
112012.m: Seed tape makes it easier to sow at even distances.

112013.q: Which plant brew is sprayed in organic gardens to prevent fungal diseases?
112013.e: Field horsetail contains lots of silica. The brew is meant to strengthen the leaf surface and make it harder for fungi to get in.
112013.m: Horsetail brew makes plants stronger against fungi.

112108.e: Real flu, also called influenza, is caused by flu viruses. Cold alone does not make you ill.
112108.m: Real flu is caused by viruses.

a: A worldwide flu wave with millions of deaths
A harmless cold only in Spain
112109.e: The Spanish flu began in 1918 towards the end of the First World War. It spread across the whole world and killed many millions of people.
112109.m: The Spanish flu was a worldwide flu wave from 1918.

112110.q: In which season are there the most cases of flu in Switzerland?
112110.e: In Switzerland the flu wave usually reaches its peak between December and March. That is why people speak of the flu season in winter.
112110.m: In Switzerland, the flu season is in winter.

112111.q: What is typical of real flu compared with an ordinary cold?
112111.e: Real flu usually starts very suddenly with a high fever, aching limbs and a strong feeling of being ill. A cold, on the other hand, usually develops more slowly and is milder.
112111.m: Flu usually starts suddenly with a high fever.

112112.q: How are flu viruses mainly passed from person to person?
112112.e: When you cough, sneeze and talk, tiny droplets with viruses get into the air and others breathe them in. The viruses can also be passed on by hands.
112112.m: Flu is mainly passed on through droplets when coughing and sneezing.

112113.q: What is the form of influenza called that mainly affects birds?
112113.e: Bird flu is caused by certain influenza A viruses that mainly affect wild birds and poultry. People only rarely catch it.
112113.m: Bird flu is an influenza that mainly makes birds ill.

112114.q: What is a disease called that spreads across the whole world?
112114.e: A pandemic is a wave of disease that affects many countries and continents. Examples are the Spanish flu and COVID-19.
112114.m: A worldwide wave of disease is called a pandemic.

112115.q: Which kind of medicine works directly against flu viruses?
112115.e: Antiviral drugs slow down the multiplication of flu viruses in the body. They work best if you take them early after the illness starts.
112115.m: Antiviral drugs can slow down the multiplication of flu viruses.

112116.q: For which age group does the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) especially recommend the flu vaccination?
112116.e: Older people more often become seriously ill with flu. That is why the FOPH recommends the vaccination for everyone over 65 and for people with chronic illnesses, among others.
112116.m: From the age of 65, the flu vaccination is especially recommended.

112117.q: Which rare but very dangerous complication can measles cause?
112117.e: In rare cases, measles can cause an inflammation of the brain that can leave lasting damage or be fatal. Middle ear infections and pneumonia are more common.
112117.m: Measles can rarely cause a dangerous inflammation of the brain.

112118.q: Which sign of illness is typical of measles?
a: Red spots all over the body with a high fever
A ring around a tick bite
112118.e: With measles you get a high fever and a red, blotchy rash that usually starts behind the ears and spreads over the body.
112118.m: Measles shows itself with fever and red spots all over the body.

112119.q: What kind of vaccine is used against measles?
a: A live vaccine with weakened viruses
A vaccine made of killed bacteria
112119.e: The measles vaccine contains live but greatly weakened measles viruses. They do not make you ill, but they train the immune system.
112119.m: Measles vaccines use weakened, live viruses.

112120.q: Why could measles be wiped out worldwide?
a: Because the virus only occurs in humans
Because the virus only lives in winter
112120.e: The measles virus has no animal hosts. If enough people are vaccinated, it finds no new victims and disappears.
112120.m: Measles could be wiped out because only humans carry the virus.

112121.q: What does measles often do to the immune system for months to years?
a: It makes you immune to all diseases
112121.e: The measles virus destroys defence cells that remember earlier germs. Afterwards, people affected catch other infections more easily.
112121.m: Measles weakens the memory of the immune system.

112122.q: What do you typically see on the skin with chickenpox?
112122.e: Chickenpox is caused by a virus. Typical are itchy, fluid-filled blisters all over the body.
112122.m: Chickenpox causes itchy blisters on the skin.

112123.q: Where does the German name for chickenpox, “Windpocken” (wind pox), come from?
a: The viruses are spread far through the air
You only get them in a storm
They heal faster in the wind
112123.e: The name shows that the viruses can be carried several metres with the air we breathe out. So they spread, as it were, with the wind.
112123.m: In German, chickenpox is called wind pox because it spreads far through the air.

112124.q: Until when is a child with chickenpox contagious?
a: Until all the blisters have crusted over
112124.e: The fluid in the blisters contains many viruses. Only when all the blisters have dried up and crusted over are you no longer contagious.
112124.m: With chickenpox you are contagious until all the blisters have crusted over.

112125.q: What should you try not to do when you have chickenpox?
112125.e: Scratched blisters can become infected and leave scars. Short fingernails and cooling remedies for the itching help.
112125.m: You should not scratch chickenpox blisters.

112126.q: Who discovered the germ that causes tuberculosis in 1882?
112126.e: The German doctor Robert Koch presented his discovery in Berlin in 1882. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it in 1905.
112126.m: Robert Koch discovered the tuberculosis germ in 1882.

a: Yes, it is one of the most common deadly infectious diseases worldwide
No, it was wiped out 100 years ago
112127.e: Every year, millions of people worldwide fall ill with tuberculosis, mainly in poorer countries. In Switzerland it has become rare.

112128.q: Which organ does tuberculosis affect most often?
112128.e: Tuberculosis of the lungs is the most common. But the bacteria can also affect bones, lymph nodes or other organs.
112128.m: Tuberculosis most often affects the lungs.

112129.e: Against tuberculosis, several antibiotics are taken at the same time for at least six months. This stops the bacteria from becoming resistant.
112129.m: Tuberculosis is treated for months with several antibiotics.

112130.q: Which place in the Grisons became famous in the 19th century for its health resorts for people with lung disease?
112130.e: From about 1865, many sanatoriums were built in Davos because people believed the mountain air helped with tuberculosis. That is how the place became a well-known health resort.
112130.m: Davos became famous as a health resort for people with lung disease.

112131.q: What was tuberculosis commonly called in the past?
112131.e: Because the sick became very thin and slowly “wasted away”, people used to call it consumption.
112131.m: Tuberculosis used to be called consumption.

112132.q: Are all children in Switzerland vaccinated against tuberculosis today?
a: There is no vaccine against it at all
112132.e: There is a vaccine against tuberculosis, the BCG vaccine. Because the disease is rare in Switzerland, it is now only recommended in special cases.
112132.m: In Switzerland, people are only vaccinated against tuberculosis in special cases.

112133.q: How is tuberculosis usually passed on?
112133.e: People with active tuberculosis of the lungs cough bacteria into the air. Others breathe them in and can become infected.
112133.m: Tuberculosis is passed on through the air we breathe.

a: The bacteria do not respond to several antibiotics
The bacteria live in several countries
112134.e: With multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, the most important standard medicines no longer work. Treatment is then much longer and more difficult.
112134.m: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis cannot be cured with the usual antibiotics.

112135.q: Which animal passes malaria on to humans?
112135.e: Malaria is passed on by the bite of mosquitoes of the genus Anopheles. They take in the germs when sucking blood and pass them on.
112135.m: Malaria is passed on by Anopheles mosquitoes.

112136.q: What does the Italian expression “mala aria”, which malaria comes from, mean?
112136.e: People used to believe the disease came from bad air from swamps. That is where the name malaria comes from.

112137.q: Which Anopheles mosquitoes bite and pass on malaria?
112137.e: Only female mosquitoes suck blood, because they need it for their eggs to develop. Males feed on plant juices.
112137.m: Only female Anopheles mosquitoes pass on malaria.

112138.q: Which sign of illness is typical of malaria?
a: A red ring around the bite
Loss of the sense of smell
112138.e: With malaria, bouts of fever with shivering often occur at regular intervals. They happen when many infected blood cells burst at the same time.
112138.m: Malaria causes repeated attacks of fever.

112139.q: In which region of the world are there the most cases of malaria?
a: In Africa south of the Sahara
112139.e: Most malaria cases and deaths are in countries in Africa south of the Sahara. Young children are especially at risk.
112139.m: Most malaria cases are in Africa south of the Sahara.

112140.q: Which plant does the old malaria medicine quinine come from?
112140.e: Quinine is obtained from the bark of the cinchona tree from South America. For a long time it was the most important medicine against malaria.
112140.m: Quinine from cinchona bark was long the most important malaria medicine.

112141.q: Which simple item protects especially well against malaria at night?
a: A mosquito net over the bed
112141.e: Anopheles mosquitoes mainly bite at dusk and at night. A mosquito net treated with insecticide keeps them away from the sleeper.
112141.m: A mosquito net protects against malaria mosquitoes at night.

112142.q: In which blood cells do the malaria germs multiply?
a: In the blood plasma without cells
112142.e: After a phase in the liver, the plasmodia enter red blood cells, multiply there and make them burst.
112142.m: Malaria germs multiply in the red blood cells.

112143.q: What kind of germ causes malaria?
112143.e: Malaria is caused by tiny single-celled parasites called plasmodia. The mosquito passes them into the blood when it bites.
112143.m: Malaria is caused by single-celled parasites.

112144.q: What kind of germ causes cholera?
112144.e: Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae.
112144.m: Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae.

112145.q: What is the main feature of cholera?
112145.e: The toxin of the cholera bacteria causes very severe, watery diarrhoea in the gut. You can lose many litres of fluid a day.
112145.m: Cholera causes very severe, watery diarrhoea.

112146.q: How do people usually catch cholera?
112146.e: Cholera bacteria get into the water through the waste of sick people. Anyone who drinks contaminated water or eats food washed in it can become infected.
112146.m: Cholera mainly spreads through dirty water.

112147.q: In 1854 in London, how did a doctor find out that cholera came from the water of a pump?
a: He marked the cases of illness on a map of the city
He counted the rats in the streets
112147.e: The doctor John Snow marked all the cholera cases on a city map. They were clustered around a water pump in Broad Street.
112147.m: A city map with all the cases showed that cholera spreads through water.

112148.q: What is most important in treating cholera?
112148.e: The loss is made up with a drink made of water, sugar and salts, or with drips. That way almost everyone who is treated survives.
112148.m: With cholera, above all fluids and salts must be replaced.

112149.q: What do untreated cholera patients usually die of?
a: The body's huge loss of water
A heart attack caused by fever
112149.e: The diarrhoea dries out the body, the blood becomes thick and the circulation fails. Without treatment this can be fatal within hours.
112149.m: Cholera is dangerous because the body dries out.

112150.q: In the 19th century, which measure helped most against cholera in European cities?
112150.e: Once it was understood that the disease got into drinking water through sewage, many cities built sewers and safe water pipes. After that the outbreaks fell sharply.
112150.m: Sewers and clean water drove cholera out of Europe's cities.

112151.q: How is the cholera vaccine given?
a: As an oral vaccine you swallow
112151.e: The cholera vaccine is drunk so that it works directly in the gut, where the bacteria attack.
112151.m: There is an oral vaccine against cholera.

a: They are curved like a comma
112152.e: Vibrio cholerae is a slightly curved rod that looks like a comma. With a long whip-like tail it can move quickly.
112152.m: Cholera bacteria look like a comma.

112153.q: What is the virus called that causes COVID-19?
112153.e: COVID-19 is caused by the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2. It is related to the SARS virus of 2002.
112153.m: COVID-19 is caused by the virus SARS-CoV-2.

112154.q: In which city was COVID-19 first detected at the end of 2019?
112154.e: The first cases of the new lung disease became known in December 2019 in Wuhan in China. From there the virus spread worldwide.
112154.m: COVID-19 was first discovered in Wuhan at the end of 2019.

112155.q: What does it mean that COVID-19 was a pandemic?
a: The disease spread across the whole world
The disease only existed in one village
The disease only occurred in summer
112155.e: A pandemic is a disease that spreads across many countries and continents. In March 2020, COVID-19 was officially declared a pandemic.
112155.m: A pandemic is the worldwide spread of a disease.

112156.q: What did the Federal Council close throughout Switzerland in March 2020 because of COVID-19?
112156.e: In March 2020 the Federal Council declared an extraordinary situation. Schools and many shops were closed; food shops and hospitals stayed open.
112156.m: In March 2020, schools in Switzerland were closed.

112157.q: Which variant of SARS-CoV-2 spread especially quickly worldwide from the end of 2021?
112157.e: The Omicron variant was first reported in November 2021 and within a few weeks pushed out the earlier variants. The WHO named the variants with Greek letters.
112157.m: From the end of 2021, the Omicron variant took over worldwide.

112158.q: Which document did adults in Switzerland have to show at times in 2021, for example to eat in a restaurant?
112158.e: The COVID certificate confirmed a vaccination, recovery or a negative test. It was shown as a QR code on a phone or on paper.
112158.m: The COVID certificate was required in many places in 2021.

112159.q: Which new vaccine technology was used on a large scale for the first time against COVID-19?
112159.e: mRNA vaccines contain a blueprint that body cells use to make a part of the virus. That way the immune system learns to recognise the real virus.
112159.m: mRNA vaccines were widely used for the first time against COVID-19.

112160.q: What does the number 19 in “COVID-19” stand for?
112160.e: COVID stands for “coronavirus disease”. The 19 shows that it was discovered in 2019.
112160.m: The number 19 in COVID-19 stands for the year it was discovered.

112161.e: “Corona” is Latin for crown or wreath. Under the electron microscope, the viruses have wreath-like spikes on their surface.
112161.m: Coronaviruses are named after their crown-like shape.

112162.q: Which rule applied on public transport in Switzerland from July 2020?
a: Wearing a bike helmet was compulsory
112162.e: From 6 July 2020, masks had to be worn on trains, trams and buses throughout Switzerland. Later the rule was extended to other places.
112162.m: From July 2020, masks were compulsory on public transport in Switzerland.

112163.q: What was the federal government's app called that warned of possible COVID infections?
112163.e: The SwissCovid app used Bluetooth to detect who had been close to a person who later tested positive for a long time. It was introduced in June 2020.
112163.m: The SwissCovid app warned of possible infections.

112164.q: What is another English name for tetanus?
112164.e: Tetanus is also called lockjaw, because the germs get in through wounds and cause strong muscle cramps, often starting in the jaw.

112165.q: Where are tetanus bacteria mainly found?
112165.e: The bacterium Clostridium tetani lives in soil, in dust and in the gut of animals. It is found practically everywhere.
112165.m: Tetanus germs live almost everywhere in the soil.

112166.q: Which sign is typical of tetanus?
a: A red ring on the skin
112166.e: Tetanus often starts with a locked jaw, so you can hardly open your mouth. Later, other muscles all over the body cramp up.
112166.m: Tetanus often starts with cramped jaw muscles.

112167.q: After a dirty wound, for example from a fall on soil, what should you check?
a: Whether your tetanus vaccination is still valid
Whether your blood group is right
Whether you are allergic to pollen
Whether you have had enough vitamin C
112167.e: Tetanus germs get into the body through dirty wounds. That is why you should look in your vaccination record to see whether you need a booster.
112167.m: After dirty wounds, you check your tetanus protection.

112168.q: Can you catch tetanus from a person who has it?
112168.e: Tetanus is not passed from person to person. You only catch it through dirty wounds, so only your own vaccination protects you.
112168.m: Tetanus is not contagious from person to person.

112169.q: What causes the cramps in tetanus?
a: A poison made by the bacteria
Too much sugar in the blood
112169.e: The bacteria make a strong nerve poison called tetanospasmin. It disturbs the control of the muscles, which then cramp up all the time.
112169.m: A nerve poison from tetanus bacteria causes the cramps.

112170.q: In what form do tetanus germs survive in the soil for years?
112170.e: The bacteria form very tough spores that can withstand heat and drought for a long time. In a wound they start to grow again.
112170.m: Tetanus germs survive in the soil as spores.

112171.q: Together with which other disease is the tetanus vaccine usually given to adults?
112171.e: In Switzerland, the tetanus vaccine is usually given as a combined vaccine with diphtheria, often also with whooping cough.
112171.m: Tetanus is usually vaccinated against together with diphtheria.

112172.q: Are you immune after you have recovered from tetanus?
a: No, you still need to be vaccinated
112172.e: Even a tiny amount of tetanus poison is enough to cause the disease, but too little to build up protection. That is why you need a vaccination even after the illness.
112172.m: After tetanus you are not immune and need a vaccination.

112173.q: What kind of germ causes Lyme disease?
112173.e: The germs that cause Lyme disease are corkscrew-shaped bacteria called Borrelia. That is why the disease can be treated with antibiotics.
112173.m: Lyme disease is caused by bacteria called Borrelia.

112174.e: Because Borrelia are bacteria, the disease is treated with antibiotics. The earlier treatment starts, the better.
112174.m: Lyme disease is treated with antibiotics.

112175.q: Why should you remove a tick as quickly as possible?
a: Because Borrelia are usually only passed on after hours
Because otherwise the tick lays eggs in the skin
Because otherwise it moves into the body
112175.e: The Borrelia sit in the tick's gut and usually only get into the skin after many hours of sucking. Removing the tick quickly lowers the risk a lot.
112175.m: A tick that is removed quickly passes on Lyme disease less often.

112176.q: Which place is Lyme disease named after?
112176.e: In the 1970s, a cluster of joint inflammation in children was noticed in the area around Lyme in the US state of Connecticut. The disease was named after it.
112176.m: Lyme disease is named after the town of Lyme in the USA.

112177.q: Where in Switzerland can you catch Lyme disease?
112177.e: Ticks carrying Borrelia are found throughout Switzerland, especially in woods, at the edges of woods and in long grass, up to medium altitudes.
112177.m: You can catch Lyme disease almost anywhere in Switzerland.

112178.q: Which long-term effect can untreated Lyme disease have?
112178.e: If the infection is not treated, joints, especially the knees, can swell months later. Nerves and the heart can also be affected.
112178.m: Untreated Lyme disease can lead to inflamed joints.

112179.q: Which group of animals do ticks belong to?
112179.e: Like mites, ticks belong to the arachnids and not to the insects, even though they are often thought to be insects.

112180.q: As of 2025, was there an approved vaccine against Lyme disease for humans in Switzerland?
a: No, you mainly protect yourself against tick bites
Yes, it is compulsory for all children
Yes, it is in the basic vaccination plan
Yes, it is given together with measles
112180.e: Unlike for TBE, there was no approved vaccine against Lyme disease for humans. That is why long clothes, tick repellent and checking your body after being outdoors are important.
112180.m: Protection against tick bites is the main help against Lyme disease.

112181.q: What kind of germ causes TBE (tick-borne encephalitis)?
112181.e: TBE is caused by the TBE virus, which belongs to the flavivirus family. That is why antibiotics do not work against it.
112181.m: TBE is caused by a virus.

112182.q: For which areas does the FOPH recommend the TBE vaccination (as of 2025)?
a: For the whole of Switzerland except Ticino
Only for the canton of Zurich
112182.e: According to the FOPH, as of 2025 the whole of Switzerland except the canton of Ticino counts as a TBE risk area. The vaccination is recommended for anyone who spends time outdoors there.
112182.m: The TBE vaccination is recommended for almost the whole of Switzerland.

112183.q: What does the German abbreviation FSME, used for tick-borne encephalitis, stand for?
112183.e: In German the disease is called early-summer meningoencephalitis, because ticks are especially active from early summer and the virus can inflame the membranes around the brain and the brain itself.

112184.q: Which parts of the body can TBE inflame?
a: The membranes around the brain and the brain
112184.e: Meningitis means inflammation of the membranes around the brain; encephalitis means inflammation of the brain. In severe cases, lasting paralysis can result.
112184.m: TBE can inflame the brain and the membranes around it.

112185.q: Which statement about the treatment of TBE is true?
a: There is no medicine against the virus
112185.e: There is no effective medicine against the TBE virus itself; only the symptoms can be eased. That is why vaccination is the most important protection.
112185.m: Vaccination is the main protection against TBE, because it cannot be cured.

112186.q: What is the best way to protect yourself from TBE?
112186.e: There is no medicine against the TBE virus. Vaccination and long clothes in the woods protect best.

112187.q: Through which food can TBE also be passed on in rare cases?
112187.e: Goats, sheep or cows that have been bitten by infected ticks can pass the virus out in their milk. Heating kills it.
112187.m: Unpasteurised raw milk can rarely pass on TBE.

112188.q: Which animal usually passes the TBE virus on to humans?
112188.e: TBE is almost always passed on by tick bites. That is why you should check yourself for ticks after a trip to the woods.

112189.q: What is meant by a pandemic?
a: A disease in a single village
112189.e: In a pandemic, an infectious disease spreads across countries and continents. So it affects a great many people all over the world.
112189.m: A pandemic is a worldwide epidemic.

112190.q: What does the Greek prefix “pan” in the word pandemic mean?
112190.e: “Pan” means all or whole, and “demos” means people. So a pandemic affects, as it were, all the people.

112191.q: Which disease caused the “Black Death” in Europe in the 14th century?
112191.e: From 1347, the plague spread across Europe and killed an estimated third of the population. It is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
112191.m: The Black Death in the 14th century was the plague.

112192.q: Which organisation officially determines whether there is a pandemic?
112192.e: The World Health Organization (WHO) monitors the spread of diseases worldwide and can declare a pandemic.
112192.m: The WHO officially declares a pandemic.

112193.q: In which Swiss city does the World Health Organization have its headquarters?
112193.e: The World Health Organization was founded in 1948 and has its headquarters on Lake Geneva. Many international organisations are based there.
112193.m: The World Health Organization has its headquarters in Geneva.

112194.q: Why can diseases spread around the world faster today than in the past?
112194.e: By plane, infected people can reach other continents within a few hours. In the past, such journeys took weeks.
112194.m: Air travel lets diseases travel quickly around the world today.

112195.q: What does “flattening the curve” mean in a pandemic?
a: Spreading infections out over time so hospitals are not overwhelmed
112195.e: When fewer people are infected at the same time, the sick are spread over a longer period. That way hospitals have enough beds for everyone.
112195.m: A flat curve protects hospitals from being overwhelmed.

112196.q: Which animals mainly spread the plague?
112196.e: Plague bacteria live in rodents such as rats. When their host dies, rat fleas also bite people and pass on the disease.
112196.m: The plague was mainly spread by rat fleas.

112197.q: Why is the Spanish flu called that, even though it did not start in Spain?
a: Because Spanish newspapers were the first to report on it openly
Because a Spaniard discovered the virus
Because it came with Spanish fruit
112197.e: Spain was neutral in the First World War and did not censor its press. So the first open reports appeared there, and the epidemic got its name.
112197.m: The Spanish flu is named after the first open reports from Spain.

112198.q: Which federal office leads the measures against a pandemic in Switzerland?
a: The Federal Office of Public Health
112198.e: The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) monitors infectious diseases and has drawn up a pandemic plan for Switzerland.
112198.m: In Switzerland, the FOPH is responsible for fighting pandemics.

a: A large number of cases of a disease in a particular area and period
A disease that only one single person has
112199.e: In an epidemic, many more people than usual in a region fall ill within a short time. It is limited to one area.
112199.m: An epidemic is a disease concentrated in one place and time.

112201.q: Which federal law governs the fight against infectious diseases in Switzerland?
112201.e: The Epidemics Act sets out how the Confederation and the cantons detect, monitor and fight infectious diseases. The current version has been in force since 2016.
112201.m: In Switzerland, the Epidemics Act governs how epidemics are handled.

112202.q: What does a reproduction number R above 1 mean?
a: The number of infections is rising
The disease has been wiped out
Nobody is being infected any more
The number of cases stays exactly the same
112202.e: R tells you how many people one sick person infects on average. If R is greater than 1, each person infects more than one other and cases increase.
112202.m: With a reproduction number above 1, a disease spreads.

112203.q: One person infects 3 others, and each of them infects 3 more. How many new infections are there in this second round?
112203.e: In the first round, 3 people are infected. Each of them infects 3 more, so 3 times 3 equals 9.
112203.m: Infections grow from round to round by multiplying.

112204.q: In which region was there a large Ebola epidemic from 2014 to 2016?
112204.e: The Ebola epidemic mainly affected Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia. It was the largest Ebola outbreak up to that time.
112204.m: The large Ebola epidemic of 2014 to 2016 hit West Africa.

112205.q: What is the science that studies how diseases spread in a population called?
112205.e: Epidemiology studies how often diseases occur, who is affected and what causes them.
112205.m: Epidemiology studies the spread of diseases.

112206.q: Who must doctors in Switzerland report certain infectious diseases to?
a: The cantonal and federal health authorities
112206.e: Many infectious diseases must be reported. This allows the cantonal doctor and the FOPH to detect outbreaks early and take action.
112206.m: Notifiable infectious diseases are reported to the health authorities.

112207.q: Which part of the eye changes the size of the pupil?
112207.e: The iris is a ring-shaped muscle around the pupil. It contracts in bright light and opens in the dark.
112207.m: The iris controls the size of the pupil.

112208.q: What is the clear, jelly-like mass that fills most of the eyeball called?
112208.e: The vitreous body lies between the lens and the retina and is mostly water. It gives the eye its round shape and lets light pass through freely.
112208.m: The vitreous body fills the eyeball and keeps its shape.

112209.q: What is the place on the retina called where there are no sensory cells?
112209.e: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no light-sensitive cells. The brain fills in the gap in the picture without us noticing.
112209.m: The eye cannot see anything at the blind spot.

112210.q: What is the tough, white outer layer of the eyeball called?
112210.e: The sclera is a tough protective layer of connective tissue and forms the “white” of the eye. At the front it becomes the clear cornea.
112210.m: The sclera is the white protective layer of the eye.

112211.q: What is the eye's ability to focus sharply on near and distant objects called?
112211.e: In accommodation, the ciliary muscle changes the curve of the lens. This gives a sharp image of both near and distant things.
112211.m: The focusing of the eye is called accommodation.

112212.q: Which nerve carries the signals from the eye to the brain?
112212.e: The sensory cells of the retina turn light into electrical signals. The optic nerve carries them to the visual centre at the back of the head.
112212.m: The optic nerve connects the eye to the brain.

112213.q: Which part of a digital camera corresponds to the retina in the eye?
112213.e: As on the retina, the image forms on the image sensor, and there light is turned into electrical signals.
112213.m: A camera's image sensor corresponds to the retina.

112214.q: What is the eye problem called in which an unevenly curved cornea makes points look like lines?
112214.e: With astigmatism, the cornea bends light by different amounts in different directions. Special glasses lenses correct this.
112214.m: Astigmatism makes points look like lines.

112215.q: Which part of a camera controls how big the opening for the light is?
112215.e: The aperture is made of movable blades that form an adjustable opening in the lens. The bigger the opening, the more light reaches the sensor.
112215.m: The aperture decides how wide the camera opens for light.

112216.q: Which part of a camera decides how long light falls on the sensor?
112216.e: When you take a photo, the shutter opens for an adjustable time, the exposure time. It can range from many seconds to thousandths of a second.
112216.m: The shutter decides the exposure time.

112217.q: How does a camera focus on a nearby object?
a: The lens is moved further away from the sensor
112217.e: For nearby objects the image forms further behind the lens. So the lenses are moved further from the sensor, while the eye changes the shape of its lens instead.
112217.m: For close subjects the lens moves further from the sensor.

112219.q: How many pixels does a 24-megapixel camera sensor have?
112219.e: The prefix “mega” means million. 24 megapixels are therefore 24 times 1,000,000, which is 24 million pixels.
112219.m: One megapixel is a million pixels.

112220.q: What exposure time do you need to photograph a fast ski racer without blurring?
a: A very short one, about 1/2000 second
A very long one, about 30 seconds
112220.e: During a long exposure, the skier keeps moving in the picture and becomes blurred. A very short exposure time freezes the movement.
112220.m: Short exposure times freeze fast movement.

112221.q: What is the mirror in a single-lens reflex camera for?
a: It sends the image into the viewfinder
112221.e: Before the photo is taken, a slanted mirror reflects the image up into the viewfinder. When you press the button, it flips up so that light falls on the sensor.
112221.m: In a reflex camera, a mirror shows the image in the viewfinder.

112222.q: What does a higher ISO setting do on a digital camera?
a: The sensor becomes more sensitive, but the image grainier
The image becomes sharper and more colourful
112222.e: With a higher ISO setting, the sensor's signals are amplified more. This makes photos possible in low light, but there is more image noise.
112222.m: A high ISO helps in low light but creates image noise.

a: A single-eye telescope for watching nature
112223.e: A spotting scope is a telescope you look through with one eye. It is used mainly for watching animals and landscapes.
112223.m: A spotting scope is a single-eye telescope for nature watching.

112224.q: Why does a spotting scope show an upright image, but a simple astronomical telescope does not?
a: Because prisms in the spotting scope turn the image back round
Because the spotting scope has no lenses
Because you hold the spotting scope the wrong way round
Because the spotting scope contains only mirrors
112224.e: A telescope made of two converging lenses shows the image upside down. In a spotting scope, prisms turn the image back so that you see landscapes the right way up.
112224.m: Prisms give a spotting scope an upright image.

112225.q: Who in Switzerland often uses a spotting scope to watch ibex or chamois from a great distance?
112225.e: Gamekeepers and hunters often count and watch wild animals from several hundred metres away. The spotting scope magnifies enough to recognise animals without disturbing them.
112225.m: Gamekeepers often watch animals with a spotting scope.

112226.q: What magnification does a typical spotting scope have?
112226.e: Spotting scopes magnify much more than binoculars, usually about 20 to 60 times. This lets you make out details on animals far away.
112226.m: Spotting scopes usually magnify 20 to 60 times.

112227.q: Why do people usually put a spotting scope on a tripod?
a: Because at high magnification every shake is very visible
Because it only works at night
112227.e: A 40-times magnification also magnifies every wobble of your hands 40 times. On a tripod the image stays steady.
112227.m: Strong magnification needs a steady tripod.

112228.q: What does a zoom eyepiece on a spotting scope let you do?
112228.e: With a zoom eyepiece you can adjust the magnification by turning it, for example from 20 to 60 times. So you first find an animal in the wide field of view and then zoom in.
112228.m: A zoom eyepiece changes the magnification smoothly.

112229.q: How can you take photos of distant animals with a spotting scope?
a: You hold a phone camera behind the eyepiece
You stick a photo on the front of the lens
You look in with both eyes at once
You turn the spotting scope round the other way
112229.e: If you hold or attach a phone behind the eyepiece, it photographs the magnified image. This gives photos of distant birds or wild animals.
112229.m: With a phone and a spotting scope you can photograph distant animals.

112230.q: From which Latin verb does the German word “Spektiv” (spotting scope) come?
112230.e: “Spectare” means to look at or watch in Latin. The same word is found in “spectacle” and “perspective”.
112230.m: “Spektiv” comes from the Latin word for looking.

112231.q: A microscope has a 40x objective and a 10x eyepiece. What is the total magnification?
112231.e: The total magnification is the objective magnification multiplied by the eyepiece magnification: 40 times 10 makes 400.
112231.m: With a microscope you multiply the objective and eyepiece magnifications.

112232.q: What was Antonie van Leeuwenhoek the first to see in the 17th century with microscopes he built himself?
112232.e: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground tiny, very powerful lenses. With them he was the first to describe bacteria and other tiny living things.
112232.m: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was the first to see bacteria.

112233.q: Which term did Robert Hooke coin in 1665 when he looked at cork under the microscope?
112233.e: Robert Hooke saw small chambers in the cork that reminded him of monks' cells. So he called them cells.
112233.m: Robert Hooke gave cells their name.

112234.q: What do you put a specimen on to look at it under the microscope?
112234.e: A slide is a narrow strip of glass. The specimen is placed on it and usually covered with a thin cover slip.
112234.m: Specimens lie on a glass slide.

112235.q: Where does the light come from in an ordinary school microscope?
a: From above out of the eyepiece
From the side through the stand
112235.e: A lamp under the stage shines through the specimen. This is called transmitted light microscopy.
112235.m: In a school microscope, light shines from below through the specimen.

112236.q: Why must a specimen for a light microscope be very thin?
a: So that light can shine through it
So that it glows in colour
112236.e: The light has to pass through the specimen to reach the objective. Thick layers are not see-through and overlap in a blur.
112236.m: Specimens must be thin so that light can shine through.

112237.q: What can you see well with an ordinary light microscope?
a: Individual cells of an onion skin
112237.e: Cells are big enough for a light microscope. Atoms and molecules are far too small; for those you need completely different microscopes.
112237.m: With a light microscope you can see cells, but not atoms.

112238.q: Which microscope uses two separate light paths to show a three-dimensional image, for example of insects?
112238.e: A stereo microscope gives each eye a slightly different image. This lets you see small objects such as beetles or flowers in three dimensions.
112238.m: The stereo microscope shows small objects in 3D.

112239.q: What does the first number in the label “8 x 42” on a pair of binoculars mean?
112239.e: The first number tells you how strongly the binoculars magnify. An object looks as if it were 8 times closer.
112239.m: The first number on binoculars gives the magnification.

112240.q: What does the number 42 in the label “8 x 42” on a pair of binoculars mean?
a: The diameter of the objective lenses in millimetres
112240.e: The second number gives the diameter of the front lenses in millimetres. The bigger it is, the more light the device collects.
112240.m: The second number on binoculars gives the objective lens diameter.

112241.q: Why does the image in high-powered binoculars wobble slightly when you hold them in your hand?
a: Every small hand movement is magnified too
The light trembles in the air
The eyes are too far away
112241.e: Binoculars magnify not only the image but also every tremble of your hands. At high magnification a tripod therefore helps.
112241.m: The stronger the magnification, the more the image wobbles.

112242.q: With the same magnification, which binoculars are best for use at dusk?
112242.e: A larger objective lens diameter collects more light and gives a brighter image. At 56 mm it is the largest of the four.
112242.m: Large objective lenses make binoculars good at dusk.

112243.q: What is the main advantage of binoculars over a single-eye telescope?
a: You look comfortably with both eyes
112243.e: Binoculars are two telescopes side by side. Looking with both eyes is less tiring and gives a more three-dimensional impression.
112243.m: With binoculars you look with both eyes.

112244.q: What is the dioptre adjustment ring on binoculars for?
a: To balance out differences between the left and right eye
112244.e: Many people do not see equally sharply with both eyes. With the adjustment you set one eyepiece separately until both images are sharp.
112244.m: The dioptre adjustment fits the binoculars to both eyes.

112245.q: What are the prisms in binoculars for?
a: They turn the image the right way round
112245.e: The lenses alone would show an image that is upside down. The glass prisms reflect the light several times and turn the image back the right way.
112245.m: Prisms in binoculars turn the image the right way round.

112246.q: Why can you bend binoculars in the middle?
a: To fit them to the distance between your eyes
112246.e: Different people's eyes are different distances apart. By bending the binoculars, both eyepieces sit exactly in front of the pupils.
112246.m: The hinge fits binoculars to the distance between your eyes.

112247.q: What does a refracting telescope use to collect the light of the stars?
a: A large lens at the front
112247.e: In a refracting telescope, a large converging lens, the objective, gathers the light. Telescopes with a concave mirror are called reflecting telescopes.
112247.m: A refracting telescope collects light with a large lens.

112248.q: What is the minimum number of lenses a simple lens telescope needs?
112248.e: At the front the objective collects the light, at the back the eyepiece magnifies the image for the eye. So at least two lenses are needed.
112248.m: A telescope has an objective and an eyepiece.

112249.q: Which scientist was one of the first to point a telescope at the sky in 1609?
112249.e: Galileo built his own telescope and used it to discover craters on the Moon and four moons of Jupiter.
112249.m: Galileo discovered Jupiter's moons with a telescope.

112250.q: What focal length must the objective of a refracting telescope have compared with the eyepiece for it to magnify?
112250.e: The magnification is the focal length of the objective divided by the focal length of the eyepiece. It only magnifies if the objective has the longer focal length.
112250.m: A telescope magnifies when the objective has the longer focal length.

112251.q: Why do astronomers build telescopes with the largest possible lenses or mirrors?
112251.e: A bigger opening catches more light. This makes even very faint and distant stars visible.

112252.q: Why aren't much bigger refracting telescopes built?
a: Large lenses bend under their own weight
112252.e: A lens can only be held at its edge because the light has to pass through the middle. Very large, heavy lenses therefore sag and distort the image.
112252.m: Huge lenses lose their shape under their own weight.

112253.q: How many times more light does an objective lens 10 cm across collect than one 5 cm across?
112253.e: The light collected depends on the area of the lens, which grows with the square of the diameter. Twice the diameter gives 2 times 2, so 4 times more area.
112253.m: Double the lens diameter means four times more light.

112254.q: Which craftsmen built the first telescopes around 1600?
112254.e: Spectacle makers knew how to grind lenses. In the Netherlands one of them combined two lenses and so invented the telescope.
112254.m: The first telescopes came from spectacle makers.

112255.q: Which famous scientist built one of the first reflecting telescopes in 1668?
112255.e: Isaac Newton built a telescope with a curved mirror instead of a lens. A small slanted mirror sent the light sideways into the eyepiece.
112255.m: Isaac Newton built one of the first reflecting telescopes.

112256.q: Why are the largest telescopes in the world reflecting telescopes?
a: Mirrors can be supported from behind and built very large
Mirrors are always cheaper than glass
112256.e: A mirror can be supported over its whole back because the light does not have to pass through it. So mirrors many metres across can be built.
112256.m: Mirrors can be supported from behind and so built huge.

112257.q: Why does a reflecting telescope not produce coloured fringes like a simple lens?
a: Because all colours are reflected in the same way
Because it only uses red light
Because it has no focal length
112257.e: In a lens, blue light is refracted more strongly than red. In reflection, the same law of reflection applies to all colours, so no coloured fringes appear.
112257.m: Mirrors show all colours the same way.

112258.q: Why are large telescopes often built high up on dry desert mountains, for example in Chile?
a: The air there is clear and there is hardly any disturbing light
It is closer to the stars there
The Sun shines there at night
112258.e: At high altitude and in dry air there are hardly any clouds or haze. Far from cities, no artificial light disturbs the observations either.

112259.q: What are the main mirrors of very large telescopes often made of today?
112259.e: A mirror in one piece would be too heavy and too expensive. So many hexagonal mirror segments are lined up precisely to form one mirror surface.
112259.m: Huge telescope mirrors are made of hexagonal segments.

112260.q: Which part collects the light of the stars in a reflecting telescope?
a: A converging lens at the front of the tube
112260.e: The large main mirror curves inwards. It collects the light and focuses it at a focal point.
112260.m: In a reflecting telescope a concave mirror collects the light.

112261.q: Which metal is usually used to coat the surface of telescope mirrors?
112261.e: A very thin layer of aluminium reflects visible light very well. It is deposited as a vapour on the ground glass and renewed when needed.
112261.m: Telescope mirrors usually have a thin aluminium layer.

112262.q: What does adaptive optics correct in large telescopes?
a: The blurring caused by the shimmering of the air
The Earth's movement around the Sun
112262.e: Turbulent air makes stars twinkle and blurs images. A flexible mirror corrects these disturbances many times per second.
112262.m: Adaptive optics corrects the shimmering of the air.

112263.q: How must you put a slide into a slide projector for the picture to appear the right way?
a: Upside down and back to front
Upright and the right way round
112263.e: The lens produces an image that is upside down and reversed left to right. If you insert the slide the wrong way round, it appears correctly on the wall.
112263.m: Slides go in the wrong way round so the picture appears correctly.

112264.q: Where must the slide be for a projector to throw a magnified, sharp image on the wall?
a: Between one and two focal lengths from the lens
112264.e: If an object is between one and two focal lengths from a converging lens, a magnified, inverted, real image forms behind it.
112264.m: For a magnified image the slide sits between one and two focal lengths.

112265.q: What is the condenser in a projector for?
a: It directs the lamp light evenly through the slide
It cools the lamp with water
112265.e: The condenser is made of converging lenses between the lamp and the slide. It makes sure the whole picture is lit brightly and evenly.
112265.m: The condenser lights the slide evenly.

112266.q: What happens to the picture if you move a projector further away from the wall?
112266.e: The light rays spread out behind the lens. The further away the wall is, the bigger the picture becomes, but you have to refocus.
112266.m: A projector further away throws a bigger picture.

112267.q: What is the projector for transparent sheets, once common in schools, called?
112267.e: On an overhead projector the sheet lies on a lit glass plate. A mirror head throws the image on the wall, even in a bright room.
112267.m: The projector for transparencies is the overhead projector.

112268.q: What was an early 17th-century projector called that threw painted glass pictures on the wall?
112268.e: The magic lantern used a candle or oil lamp and lenses to throw enlarged images of painted glass plates on a wall.
112268.m: The magic lantern was an early picture projector.

112269.q: A slide 36 mm wide appears 1.8 m wide on the wall. How many times is the picture magnified?
112269.e: 1.8 m is 1800 mm. 1800 mm divided by 36 mm makes 50.
112269.m: Magnification is image size divided by object size.

112270.q: What does a contact lens rest on in the eye?
a: On the tear film over the cornea
Behind the lens of the eye
Under the eyelid in the bone
112270.e: The contact lens floats on a thin layer of tear fluid in front of the cornea. It moves slightly when you blink.
112270.m: Contact lenses float on the tear film in front of the cornea.

112271.q: Why must you not rinse contact lenses with tap water?
a: Because it can contain germs that inflame the cornea
Because tap water is too cold
112271.e: Tap water can contain tiny amoebas that attach themselves to the lens. They can cause a dangerous inflammation of the cornea.
112271.m: Contact lenses are only cleaned with special solution.

112272.q: Why should you not sleep in ordinary contact lenses?
a: Because the cornea then gets too little oxygen
Because the lenses grow at night
Because you would dream in colour
Because the lenses go dark at night
112272.e: The cornea has no blood vessels and takes oxygen directly from the air. With eyes closed and a lens on it, it gets too little.
112272.m: The cornea needs oxygen from the air.

112273.q: Which eyesight problem can contact lenses correct?
112273.e: Contact lenses bend light like glasses lenses so that a sharp image forms on the retina. Colour blindness or cataracts cannot be fixed this way.
112273.m: Contact lenses correct short- and long-sightedness.

112274.q: What advantage do contact lenses have over glasses for sport?
a: A clear field of view without frames
112274.e: Contact lenses move with the eye and have no frame. You see sharply to the side too, and nothing can slip or steam up.
112274.m: Contact lenses give a clear field of view without frames.

112275.q: What are most soft contact lenses made of today?
112275.e: Soft contact lenses are made of plastics that absorb water. This keeps them soft and lets oxygen through to the cornea. The first contact lenses around 1888 were still made of glass.
112275.m: Soft contact lenses are made of water-containing plastic.

112276.q: What is an endoscope used for?
a: To look inside the body or into hollow spaces
112276.e: An endoscope is a thin tube with optics and a light. With it you can see into body cavities or machines.
112276.m: With an endoscope you look inside hollow spaces.

112277.q: What does the Greek prefix “endo” in the word endoscope mean?
112277.e: “Endon” means inside and “skopein” means to look at. So an endoscope is a device for looking inside.

112278.q: What is the examination of the stomach with an endoscope called?
112278.e: In a gastroscopy, a flexible endoscope is pushed through the mouth and gullet into the stomach. The doctor sees the stomach lining on a screen.
112278.m: A gastroscopy shows the stomach from the inside.

112279.q: How does the light reach the tip inside the body in many endoscopes?
a: Through a hole in the skin
Through a mirror by the bed
Through a candle in the tip
112279.e: In glass fibres, light is reflected again and again off the walls. So it can be guided round bends to the tip of the endoscope.
112279.m: Glass fibres guide light even round bends.

112280.q: What are endoscopes used for outside medicine?
a: To check engines or pipes from the inside
112280.e: Technical endoscopes show damage in aircraft engines, pipelines or walls without having to take them apart.
112280.m: Technical endoscopes check machines from the inside.

112281.q: What are operations through small cuts using an endoscope and fine instruments called?
112281.e: Instead of one large cut, a few small openings for the endoscope and instruments are enough. The wounds heal faster and leave smaller scars.
112281.m: Keyhole surgery needs only small cuts.

a: A swallowable camera the size of a tablet
112282.e: The capsule is swallowed and takes many pictures on its way through the gut. These are sent wirelessly to a recording device.
112282.m: A capsule endoscope is a camera you can swallow.

112283.q: Where is the camera in modern video endoscopes?
a: At the tip of the tube
In the handle held by the doctor
112283.e: A tiny camera chip at the tip records the image directly and sends it electrically to the screen. Light is also brought to the tip through a cable.
112283.m: In video endoscopes the camera sits at the tip.

112284.q: A magnifying glass has a focal length of 5 cm. Roughly how strongly does it magnify, using a reference viewing distance of 25 cm?
112284.e: The magnification of a magnifying glass is roughly 25 cm divided by the focal length: 25 cm divided by 5 cm makes 5.
112284.m: The shorter the focal length of a magnifying glass, the more it magnifies.

112285.q: At roughly what distance do you hold a book to read it sharply and comfortably for a long time?
112285.e: At about 25 centimetres, an eye with normal sight can see sharply and comfortably for a long time. This distance is also used to work out how strongly a magnifying glass magnifies.
112285.m: Comfortable reading works at about 25 centimetres.

112286.q: What does an optical device such as a telescope actually magnify?
112286.e: How big something looks to us depends on the angle at which we see it. A telescope enlarges this visual angle; the object stays the same size.
112286.m: Optical devices enlarge the visual angle.

a: Magnification that shows no new details
112287.e: If you magnify more than the device can resolve, the image looks bigger but only blurrier. No new details become visible.
112287.m: Empty magnification only makes the image bigger, not more detailed.

112288.q: A chamois is standing 1000 m away. How close does it seem through a telescope that magnifies 20 times?
112288.e: With 20 times magnification, an object looks as if it were 20 times closer: 1000 m divided by 20 makes 50 m.
112288.m: A 20x telescope seems to bring things 20 times closer.

112289.q: A cell is 0.01 mm in size. How big does it look at 400 times magnification?
112289.e: 0.01 mm times 400 makes 4 mm. That is how big the cell looks in the microscope.
112289.m: The apparent size is the real size times the magnification.

112290.q: What is the disadvantage of a phone's digital zoom compared with an optical zoom?
a: It only enlarges pixels, without new details
It makes the picture more colourful
112290.e: Digital zoom cuts out part of the image and enlarges it by calculation. An optical zoom, on the other hand, changes the focal length and shows real details.
112290.m: Digital zoom only enlarges pixels; optical zoom shows real details.

112291.q: As a rule of thumb, a telescope's highest useful magnification is twice its aperture in millimetres. What is it for an aperture of 100 mm?
112291.e: Using the rule of thumb you work out 2 times 100 and get 200. Above that, the telescope hardly shows any extra detail.
112291.m: The highest useful magnification is about twice the aperture in millimetres.

112292.q: Which lens of a telescope faces the object being looked at?
112292.e: The objective is called that because it faces the object. It collects the light and produces an intermediate image.
112292.m: The objective is the lens on the side of the object.

112293.q: What focal length does a wide-angle lens have compared with a standard lens?
112293.e: A short focal length captures a wide angle of view. This lets a whole row of houses or a mountain panorama fit in the picture, for example.
112293.m: Wide-angle lenses have a short focal length.

112294.q: What is special about a zoom lens?
a: Its focal length can be changed
It only shows black and white
112294.e: In a zoom lens, groups of lenses move relative to each other. So you can switch between wide angle and telephoto without changing lenses.
112294.m: A zoom lens has a variable focal length.

112295.q: What is a macro lens used for?
a: For close-ups of small things such as insects
112295.e: A macro lens can focus very close up. So even small things such as flowers or beetles fill the whole picture.
112295.m: With a macro lens you photograph small things close up.

112296.q: What does it mean if a lens is “fast”?
a: It has a large opening and lets in a lot of light
112296.e: Fast lenses have a small smallest f-number, so a large opening. This makes photos possible even in low light.
112296.m: A fast lens has a large opening.

112297.q: Roughly how big is the angle of view of a fisheye lens?
112297.e: Fisheye lenses capture a very wide angle of view of around 180 degrees. Straight lines at the edge of the picture look strongly curved.

112298.q: How does the eyepiece in a microscope or telescope work?
a: Like a magnifying glass for the intermediate image
Like a mirror for the lamp
Like an aperture for the sensor
112298.e: The objective produces an intermediate image inside the device. The eyepiece magnifies this intermediate image once more for the eye, like a magnifying glass.
112298.m: The eyepiece magnifies the intermediate image like a magnifying glass.

112299.q: From which Latin word does the term “ocular” (eyepiece) come?
112299.e: “Oculus” means eye in Latin. The ocular is the lens that faces the eye.
112299.m: “Ocular” comes from the Latin word for eye.

112300.q: Where is the eyepiece on a microscope?
a: At the top, where you look in
At the bottom, directly above the lamp
On the side of the stand
112300.e: The eyepiece is the lens you look into. The objective, on the other hand, sits at the bottom, close to the specimen.
112300.m: The eyepiece is the lens next to the eye.

112301.q: A telescope has a focal length of 1200 mm. How strongly does it magnify with a 10 mm eyepiece?
112301.e: 1200 mm divided by 10 mm makes 120. So the telescope magnifies 120 times.
112301.m: Telescope magnification is objective focal length divided by eyepiece focal length.

112302.q: Why do people who wear glasses need eyepieces with a long eye relief?
a: So that they can see the whole field of view despite their glasses
So that the image becomes more colourful
So that the glasses don't steam up
112302.e: Glasses keep the eye away from the eyepiece. If the viewing point is too close to the eyepiece, you only see part of the image.
112302.m: Glasses wearers need eyepieces with a long eye relief.

112303.q: What is a measuring eyepiece with a built-in scale used for in a microscope?
a: To read off sizes in the specimen
112303.e: The scale appears sharply over the image of the specimen. After calibration you can use it to read off the size of cells.
112303.m: With a measuring eyepiece you measure sizes under the microscope.

112304.q: In which major region of Switzerland is most of the arable land?
112304.e: The Central Plateau is flat, has fertile soil and a mild climate. That is why most grain, maize and vegetables are grown there.
112304.m: The flat Central Plateau is Switzerland's breadbasket.

112305.q: Which cereal is the most important bread grain in Switzerland?
112305.e: Most bread is baked from wheat flour. Wheat contains lots of gluten, so the dough rises well.
112305.m: Our bread is mostly made with wheat.

112306.q: Why should heavy machines not drive over a wet field?
112306.e: Wet soil is squashed together under great weight. Then there are no pores for air and water, and roots and earthworms struggle.
112306.m: Compacted soil cannot breathe or take in water well.

112307.q: Which machine places seeds in the ground in even rows?
112307.e: The seed drill puts each seed at the right depth and the right distance. So the plants sprout evenly.
112307.m: The seed drill sows the grain in rows.

112308.q: Which cereal is grown in Switzerland mainly as animal feed?
112308.e: Feed barley is fed to pigs, cattle and chickens. A small part is malting barley for making beer.
112308.m: Here barley is mainly used as animal feed.

112309.q: Which tool loosens and turns over the top layer of soil in a field?
112309.e: The plough cuts open the soil and turns it over. This buries plant remains and gets the soil ready for sowing.
112309.m: The plough turns the soil before sowing.

112310.q: What does “direct drilling” mean in arable farming?
a: Sowing without ploughing the soil first
Sowing in pots in the greenhouse
112310.e: With direct drilling, the seed goes straight into soil that has not been worked, together with the remains of the previous crop. This protects soil life and saves fuel.
112310.m: With direct drilling, sowing is done without a plough.

112311.q: Which field crop is harvested whole in Switzerland, made into silage and fed to cows?
112311.e: With silage maize, the whole plant including the cobs is chopped up. Fermented in the silo, it is high-energy winter feed for cattle.
112311.m: Silage maize is an important winter feed for cows.

112312.q: Which breed of cattle from Valais is known for its “cow fights”?
112312.e: Hérens cows are small, strong and usually dark. They test their strength in cow fights, where a “queen” is crowned.
112312.m: The Hérens cows from Valais fight for the title of queen.

112313.q: As a ruminant, how many stomach chambers does a cow have?
112313.e: Cows have a rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. In the rumen, bacteria break down the grass, which is then chewed again.
112313.m: A cow digests its grass with four stomach chambers.

112314.q: What is a castrated male cattle animal called?
112314.e: A bull is a male cattle animal that has not been castrated. Oxen are calmer and used to pull carts and ploughs.
112314.m: An ox is a castrated male cattle animal.

112315.q: Which white goat breed from the Bernese Oberland is kept around the world as a dairy goat?
112315.e: The Saanen goat comes from the Saanenland area. It gives a particularly large amount of milk and is therefore kept all over the world.
112315.m: The Saanen goat is a world-famous dairy goat from the Bernese Oberland.

112316.q: Why does a cow give milk at all?
a: Because she has had a calf
Because she eats lots of grass
Because she is older than one year
112316.e: Like all mammals, a cow makes milk for her young. For her to give milk, she must first have had a calf.
112316.m: A cow gives milk after she has had a calf.

112317.q: Why do cattle in Switzerland wear ear tags with a number?
a: So that every animal can be traced
So that they do not get ill
112317.e: Every cattle animal is recorded with its number in the animal movement database. So you always know where an animal was born and where it lives, which is important when there are epidemics.
112317.m: Thanks to the ear tag, every cattle animal can be traced.

112318.q: Which brown cattle breed has traditionally been widespread in the Swiss mountains?
112318.e: Swiss Brown cattle come from central and eastern Switzerland. They are tough and well suited to mountain areas.
112318.m: Swiss Brown is a typical Swiss mountain breed.

112319.q: Which Bernese valley do the red and white spotted Simmental cattle come from?
112319.e: Simmental cattle are named after the Simmental valley in the Bernese Oberland. Today the breed is kept all over the world.
112319.m: Simmental cattle come from the Simmental valley.

112320.q: How many times a day are dairy cows usually milked?
112320.e: Dairy cows are usually milked in the morning and evening. With milking robots, the cows go to be milked on their own and sometimes more often.
112320.m: Dairy cows are usually milked morning and evening.

112321.q: Which zone does the federal government put steep, high farming areas in?
112321.e: Farmland is divided into the valley zone, hill zone and mountain zones I to IV. The higher the zone, the harder the farming.
112321.m: The higher the mountain zone, the harder the farmer's work.

112322.q: Which mountain zone has the most difficult conditions?
112322.e: Mountain zone IV covers the highest and steepest places. There the growing season is short and much of the work can only be done by hand.
112322.m: Mountain zone IV is the toughest zone for farming.

112323.q: Which vehicle with a low centre of gravity do mountain farmers use to mow steep slopes?
112323.e: Two-axle mowers and motor mowers are built low and wide. So they are less likely to tip over on a steep slope.
112323.m: On steep slopes, mountain farmers mow with a low-built mower.
