Great hunger and a good mood
Warm, dry skin and deep sleep
112846.e: The body draws blood away from the skin and limbs to supply the vital organs. That is why the skin becomes pale and cold, and the heart beats faster.
112846.m: Pale, cold skin and a fast pulse point to shock.

112847.q: How do you position a person showing signs of shock after blood loss, if no injuries rule it out?
a: Flat on their back with the legs slightly raised
On their front with the head raised
112847.e: In the shock position, blood flows from the legs back to the body and the vital organs. With some injuries or breathing difficulties, however, this position is not suitable.
112847.m: In shock, lay the person flat with legs slightly raised, if nothing rules it out.

112848.q: What do people with a severe wasp sting allergy often carry with them?
112848.e: After a sting, life-threatening allergic shock can develop. With the emergency pen, you inject yourself with adrenaline immediately.
112848.m: People with allergies carry an adrenaline pen for emergencies.

112849.q: Apart from calling for help, what do you do for a person in shock?
a: Cover them, calm them and do not leave them alone
112849.e: Keeping warm, calming down and being looked after help the body to stabilise the circulation. Until the ambulance arrives, you keep checking breathing and consciousness.
112849.m: Cover people in shock, calm them and stay with them.

112850.q: What is shock caused by a large loss of blood or fluid called?
112850.e: If a lot of blood or fluid is missing, there is too little volume in the circulation. This form of shock is called hypovolaemic shock.
112850.m: Hypovolaemic shock is caused by missing blood or fluid in the circulation.

112851.q: Why should a person showing signs of shock not eat or drink anything?
a: They may need an operation and could vomit
They would get better too quickly
112851.e: Shock may make an anaesthetic or operation necessary, for which the stomach should be as empty as possible. Also, their condition can get worse and the person can vomit.
112851.m: In shock, give nothing to eat and nothing to drink.

112852.q: With which injury must you not raise the legs of a person in shock?
a: An insect sting on the arm
112852.e: Raising a broken leg causes pain and can make the injury worse. The shock position is also unsuitable for head injuries or breathing difficulties.
112852.m: With leg injuries, do not raise the legs.

112853.q: What does the A in the ABC approach of first aid stand for?
112853.e: A stands for airway. It must be open so that any air can get into the lungs at all.
112853.m: A stands for airway and comes first in an emergency.

112854.q: What does the C in the ABC approach stand for?
112854.e: For C, you check and secure the blood circulation. This includes, for example, chest compressions or stopping heavy bleeding.
112854.m: In the ABC approach, C stands for circulation.

112855.q: Which language do the terms behind the letters of the ABC approach come from?
112855.e: The letters stand for Airway, Breathing and Circulation. The approach is used in many countries, including Switzerland.
112855.m: The ABC approach comes from English.

112856.q: Why are the steps of the ABC approach checked in exactly this order?
a: Because the greatest danger to life is dealt with first
Because they must be in alphabetical order
Because the order was chosen at random
112856.e: Without an open airway, breathing is no use, and without oxygen in the blood, the circulation does not help much either. So the order follows urgency.
112856.m: In the ABC approach, the most life-threatening thing comes first.

112857.q: Which extension of the ABC approach do ambulance services often use?
112857.e: The ABCDE approach adds D for neurological problems such as consciousness and E for examining the whole body.
112857.m: Professionals extend the ABC approach to the ABCDE approach.

112858.q: What do you check for B in the ABC approach?
a: Whether the person is breathing normally
112858.e: B is about breathing. You look, listen and feel whether the person is breathing normally, and give rescue breaths if necessary.
112858.m: B in the ABC approach is about breathing.

112859.q: What are the three basic steps that Swiss first aid courses use to sum up what to do at the scene of an accident?
112859.e: First you get an overview, then you consider what dangers there are and what needs to be done. Only after that do you act.
112859.m: At an accident: look, think and then act.

112860.q: What always comes first, before the ABC approach, when you arrive at the scene of an accident?
a: Paying attention to your own safety
Giving the injured person something to drink
112860.e: If you put yourself in danger, you cannot help anyone any more. That is why you first secure the scene, for example with a high-visibility vest and a warning triangle.
112860.m: At an accident, your own safety comes first.

112861.q: What has the umbrella organisation of the Samaritan associations in Switzerland been called since 2022?
112861.e: The former Swiss Samaritan Federation has been called Samariter Schweiz since 2022. Hundreds of Samaritan associations all over Switzerland belong to it.
112861.m: Switzerland’s Samaritan associations are organised in Samariter Schweiz.

112862.q: Which story does the word Samaritan go back to?
a: The parable of the Good Samaritan in the Bible
A town in the canton of Valais
112862.e: In the parable from the Gospel of Luke, a man from Samaria helps someone who has been attacked and whom others have walked past. The Samaritan thus became a symbol of helpfulness.
112862.m: Samaritans are named after the helpful man in the Bible.

112863.q: Which task do Samaritans often take on at festivals and sports events?
112863.e: Samaritan associations run first aid posts at many events. They treat minor injuries and give first aid until the ambulance arrives.
112863.m: Samaritans give first aid at events.

112864.q: Which large aid organisation is Samariter Schweiz linked to?
112864.e: Samariter Schweiz is one of the Red Cross rescue organisations and follows the principles of the Red Cross movement. Together they work for first aid among the population.
112864.m: Samariter Schweiz belongs to the Swiss Red Cross family.

112865.q: How do most Samaritans in Switzerland work?
112865.e: Members of Samaritan associations help in their free time. They regularly take further training in first aid.
112865.m: Samaritans help as volunteers in their free time.

112866.q: What are the youth groups of the Samaritans in Switzerland called?
112866.e: The Help Samaritan youth was founded in Basel in 1968. In the groups, children and young people learn first aid through play.
112866.m: The youth groups of the Swiss Samaritans are called Help.

112867.q: How long has there been a joint federation of Samaritan associations in Switzerland?
112867.e: In 1888, the first Samaritan associations founded the Swiss Samaritan Federation. Since 2022 it has been called Samariter Schweiz.
112867.m: The Samaritan federation has existed for more than 100 years.

112868.q: What do you need a first aid course for in Switzerland?
a: To apply for a learner driver’s permit
112868.e: Anyone in Switzerland who wants to learn to drive a car or ride a motorbike must show they have done a first aid course before getting a learner’s permit. The course teaches the basics of first aid.
112868.m: In Switzerland, you need a first aid course for a learner driver’s permit.

112869.q: What do you learn in a first aid course?
a: First aid in accidents and emergencies
112869.e: In a first aid course you learn, for example, how to secure the scene of an accident, make an emergency call and do chest compressions.
112869.m: In a first aid course, you learn first aid.

112870.q: Which object is used in the first aid course to secure the scene of an accident on the road?
112870.e: The warning triangle warns approaching vehicles of the accident. It is best to wear a highly visible high-visibility vest as well.
112870.m: A warning triangle warns other road users of an accident.

112871.q: When may you pull an injured person out of a car after an accident?
a: Only if there is acute danger, for example fire
Never, not even if there is a fire
112871.e: You only move an injured person if they are in danger. For this, you learn the Rautek rescue grip in the first aid course.
112871.m: Only move injured people if there is acute danger.

112872.q: Which number reaches Tox Info Suisse in Switzerland in cases of poisoning?
112872.e: Tox Info Suisse gives advice on poisoning around the clock on the emergency number 145. If symptoms are serious, you still call 144.
112872.m: For poisoning, the number 145 gives you advice.

112873.q: Which European emergency number also works in Switzerland?
112873.e: 112 is valid throughout Europe and in Switzerland is passed on to the police. 911 is used in the USA and 999 in Great Britain.

112875.q: Who hangs up first in an emergency call?
112875.e: The control centre often has more questions or gives instructions, for example on chest compressions. That is why you wait until they end the call.
112875.m: In an emergency call, the control centre ends the conversation.

112876.q: How can you tell that a person has choked and cannot get any air?
a: They clutch their throat and cannot speak
112876.e: If the airway is completely blocked, the person can neither speak, cough nor breathe. Clutching the throat is typical.
112876.m: Anyone who clutches their throat and cannot speak may be choking.

112877.q: What should a person do who has choked on something but can still cough strongly?
112877.e: Strong coughing is the best way to get an object out of the airway. You encourage the person to do so and stay with them.
112877.m: Anyone who can still cough should keep coughing hard.

112878.q: What do you do first if an adult has choked and can no longer cough effectively?
a: Give firm blows between the shoulder blades
Give them bread to swallow after it
Lay them on their back and wait
112878.e: You bend the person’s upper body forwards and strike firmly between the shoulder blades with the flat of your hand. If that does not help, the Heimlich manoeuvre follows.
112878.m: First come firm blows between the shoulder blades.

112879.q: How do you position a baby for back blows if it has choked?
a: Face down on the forearm with the head lower
Hanging upside down by the feet
112879.e: The baby lies on its tummy along the forearm, with the head supported and lower than the body. Gravity then helps to free the object.
112879.m: For back blows, lay babies face down on the forearm with the head lower.

112880.q: Which small objects are a particularly common choking risk for toddlers?
112880.e: Small, round, hard things fit exactly into a toddler’s windpipe. That is why people advise keeping nuts and small parts away from toddlers.
112880.m: Nuts and small parts do not belong in toddlers’ hands.

112881.q: Why should a person still be checked by a doctor after choking has been successfully cleared?
a: Bits could be in the lungs or injuries could have occurred
Because otherwise they will get a fever
Because otherwise they will not be able to swallow any more
112881.e: Small remains may have slipped into the lungs. Also, back blows or thrusts into the upper abdomen can cause internal injuries.
112881.m: After a choking emergency, a doctor should take a look.

112882.q: What do you do if a person with an object in their airway becomes unconscious?
a: Lay them down, call for help and start resuscitation
Hold them upright and shake them
Leave them alone and go to get help
112882.e: If the person becomes unconscious, you lay them on the floor and start chest compressions. The compressions can also free the object.
112882.m: If a choking person becomes unconscious, start resuscitation.

112883.q: When do you use the Heimlich manoeuvre?
a: When someone is in danger of choking on something they have swallowed
112883.e: If an object is stuck in the airway and the person can no longer breathe or cough, the Heimlich manoeuvre can push it out. It is named after the US doctor Henry Heimlich.
112883.m: The Heimlich manoeuvre helps when someone is in danger of choking.

112884.q: Where do you place your fist for the Heimlich manoeuvre?
a: In the upper abdomen between the belly button and the tip of the breastbone
On the back over the kidneys
112884.e: The helper stands behind the person, puts their arms around them and places the fist in the upper abdomen. Then they pull sharply inwards and upwards.
112884.m: In the Heimlich manoeuvre, the fist presses into the upper abdomen.

112885.q: How does the Heimlich manoeuvre work?
a: The pressure on the diaphragm forces air out of the lungs
It stimulates the stomach to digest
It lowers blood pressure in the head
112885.e: The sudden thrust pushes the diaphragm upwards. The air from the lungs shoots out and pushes the object out like a cork.
112885.m: In the Heimlich manoeuvre, air from the lungs pushes the object out.

112886.q: On whom must you not use the Heimlich manoeuvre?
112886.e: In babies, the risk of injuring the abdominal organs is too great. Instead of upper abdominal thrusts, chest thrusts with two fingers are used for them.
112886.m: For babies, chest thrusts replace the Heimlich manoeuvre.

112887.q: Where does the helper stand when doing the Heimlich manoeuvre on an adult?
a: Next to the person lying down
On a chair above the person
112887.e: The helper stands behind the person and puts both arms around them. That way they can pull strongly inwards and upwards.
112887.m: In the Heimlich manoeuvre, you stand behind the person.

112888.q: How many times at most do you repeat the Heimlich manoeuvre in one go before giving back blows again?
112888.e: According to the guidelines, up to 5 back blows and up to 5 abdominal thrusts alternate. Each time you check whether the object has come out.
112888.m: Back blows and Heimlich thrusts alternate in series of five.

112889.q: Which method is recommended instead of the Heimlich manoeuvre for very overweight people or pregnant women?
112889.e: With pregnant women and very overweight people, you cannot safely get your arms around the upper abdomen. That is why you press on the lower chest instead.
112889.m: For pregnant women, press on the chest instead of the tummy.

112890.q: Someone has choked on something but can still cough. What should the person do?
a: Quickly eat a piece of bread
112890.e: As long as the person can cough, coughing is the best way to free the object. Only when they can no longer cough or breathe are back blows and the Heimlich manoeuvre needed.
112890.m: Anyone who has choked but can still cough should cough hard.

112891.q: What do you learn in a Samaritans course?
112891.e: Samaritan associations offer courses in first aid, for example the emergency first aid course. There you learn what to do in an accident.
112891.m: With the Samaritans you learn first aid.

112892.q: What do people say in everyday life when food goes into the windpipe instead of the gullet?
a: It went down the wrong way
112892.e: When food or drink gets into the windpipe, it has gone down the wrong way. Usually you cough it back up.
112892.m: When something goes down the wrong way, it gets into the windpipe.

112893.q: How deep do you press the chest in during chest compressions on a child?
a: About a third of the depth of the chest
About half the depth of the chest
Not at all, just stroke it
112893.e: In children and babies, the depth of pressing depends on the body. You press the chest in by about a third of its depth.
112893.m: In children, press the chest in by about a third.

112894.q: Which metabolic problem can lead to unconsciousness in people with diabetes?
112894.e: If blood sugar drops sharply, the brain gets too little energy. People affected can shake, become confused and finally lose consciousness.

112895.q: Which degree of burn only affects the top layer of skin and shows as redness?
112895.e: In a first degree burn, only the outer skin is affected. The skin is red and painful, but usually heals without scars.
112895.m: A first degree burn is painful redness without blisters.

112896.q: What colour do the lips of a person who lacks oxygen turn?
112896.e: If there is a lack of oxygen in the blood, the lips and fingernails turn bluish. In medicine, this discolouration is called cyanosis.
112896.m: Blue lips are a warning sign of lack of oxygen.

112897.q: What is a measuring instrument for finding the strength of a magnetic field called?
112897.e: A magnetometer measures the strength and often also the direction of a magnetic field. A barometer, on the other hand, measures air pressure, and a hygrometer measures humidity.
112897.m: You measure magnetic fields with a magnetometer.

112898.q: Which pole of a compass needle points roughly north?
a: The north pole of the needle
The south pole of the needle
112898.e: The north pole of the compass needle points north. In reality there is a magnetic south pole of the Earth there, which attracts it.
112898.m: The north pole of the compass needle points north.

112899.q: How many millitesla are there in 1 tesla?
112899.e: The prefix milli means one thousandth. So 1 tesla is exactly 1000 millitesla.
112899.m: One tesla is a thousand millitesla.

112900.q: Which medical machine uses a very strong magnetic field to take pictures of the inside of the body?
112900.e: The magnetic resonance imaging scanner, MRI for short, uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves. It works without X-rays.
112900.m: An MRI scanner uses strong magnetic fields to take pictures of the inside of the body.

112901.q: Why must you take off all iron objects before an MRI scan?
a: The strong magnetic field would pull them violently
Iron starts to melt in the machine
112901.e: The magnetic field of an MRI scanner is tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth's. Iron objects could be pulled into the machine like bullets.
112901.m: Iron has no place near an MRI scanner.

112902.q: Which particles are pushed off their path by a magnetic field?
112902.e: In a magnetic field, a force acts on moving charges such as electrons at right angles to their direction of motion. This force is called the Lorentz force.

112903.q: What can you use to shield a magnetic field well?
a: A thick casing made of iron
112903.e: Iron gathers the field lines into itself and guides them around the inside. Paper, plastic and wood let magnetic fields through almost freely.
112903.m: Magnetic fields are shielded with iron.

112904.q: How does a magnet's magnetic field change as you move further away from it?
a: It quickly gets weaker with increasing distance
112904.e: The strength of a magnetic field drops quickly with distance from the magnet. That is why magnets only have a noticeable effect at short range.
112904.m: The further from the magnet, the weaker its field.

112905.q: In which direction do the magnetic field lines run outside a bar magnet?
a: From the north pole to the south pole
From the south pole to the north pole
Every which way, with no direction
112905.e: It has been agreed that outside the magnet, field lines point from the north pole to the south pole. Inside the magnet they continue to the north pole and close up.
112905.m: Outside the magnet, field lines run from north to south.

112906.q: What is always true of magnetic field lines?
a: They always end in empty space
They only start at the south pole
112906.e: At every point the magnetic field has exactly one direction. If two field lines crossed, there would be two directions there, which is impossible.

112907.q: On a field line diagram, how can you tell where the magnetic field is especially strong?
a: The field lines are close together there
The field lines are especially long there
The field lines are drawn in red there
There are no field lines there at all
112907.e: The density of the field lines shows the strength of the field. At the poles of a magnet they are especially close together.
112907.m: Dense field lines mean a strong magnetic field.

112908.q: What shape are the field lines around a long, straight wire carrying a current?
a: Straight lines parallel to the wire
Stars pointing away from the wire
112908.e: The field lines surround the wire in circles with the wire at their centre. The closer to the wire, the stronger the field.
112908.m: Around a straight current-carrying wire the field lines form circles.

112909.q: Which rule helps you find the direction of the field lines around a current-carrying wire?
112909.e: If the thumb of your right hand points in the conventional direction of the current, your curled fingers show the direction of the field lines.
112909.m: You use your right hand to find the direction of the field lines around a wire.

112910.q: Who introduced the idea of field lines into physics?
112910.e: In the 19th century the Englishman Michael Faraday described magnetic forces with lines of force. This easy-to-picture idea still shapes physics today.
112910.m: Michael Faraday made field lines easy to picture.

112911.q: What is a magnetic field called whose field lines are parallel and equally dense?
112911.e: In a uniform field the magnetic field is equally strong and points the same way everywhere. Such a field is found, for example, roughly between the poles of a wide horseshoe magnet.
112911.m: Parallel, equally dense field lines mark a uniform field.

112913.q: In terms of physics, which magnetic pole lies near the geographic North Pole?
112913.e: The north pole of the compass needle is attracted, so there must be a magnetic south pole in the north. It is nevertheless often called the Arctic magnetic pole or the magnetic North Pole.
112913.m: In the geographic north there is, in physics terms, a magnetic south pole.

112914.q: In which part of the Earth is the Earth's magnetic field produced by currents of liquid metal?
112914.e: Molten iron moves in the liquid outer core. Like a giant dynamo, these currents produce the magnetic field; this is called the geodynamo.
112914.m: The geodynamo in the outer core produces the Earth's magnetic field.

112915.q: What is the event called in which the Earth's magnetic north and south poles swap places?
112915.e: In the Earth's history the magnetic field has reversed many times. Traces of this can be found in solidified rock on the sea floor.
112915.m: In a magnetic reversal, the Earth's magnetic poles swap places.

112916.q: Directly above one of the Earth's magnetic poles, which way does the needle of a freely moving compass point?
112916.e: At the magnetic pole the field lines run straight down into the Earth. A freely turning needle therefore stands vertically, and an ordinary compass is useless there.
112916.m: At the magnetic pole the field lines are vertical.

112917.q: What is the region around the Earth in which the Earth's magnetic field acts called?
112917.e: The magnetosphere reaches far out into space. It steers a large part of the charged particles of the solar wind around the Earth.
112917.m: The magnetosphere is the Earth's magnetic shield.

112918.q: According to current knowledge, what do many migratory birds use the Earth's magnetic field for?
a: To find their way on their journey
112918.e: Migratory birds can sense the Earth's magnetic field. As if with an inner compass, they find their way south and back.
112918.m: Migratory birds find their way partly by the Earth's magnetic field.

112919.q: Does the magnetic pole in the north of the Earth always stay in the same place?
a: Yes, it is always exactly at the geographic North Pole
No, it jumps to a different place every day
112919.e: The magnetic pole in the north moves a little every year. For a long time it was in northern Canada, and for decades it has been moving towards Siberia.
112919.m: The magnetic North Pole slowly wanders.

112920.q: What does magnetic declination tell you?
a: The angle between magnetic north and geographic north
The error of a broken clock
How far off a thermometer is
112920.e: The compass needle points to the magnetic pole, not to the geographic North Pole. The angle between the two directions is the declination.
112920.m: Declination is the angle between compass north and geographic north.

112921.q: Where exactly does a compass needle point?
112921.e: The needle lines up with the Earth's magnetic field. The magnetic North Pole is not exactly at the geographic North Pole, which is why there is declination.
112921.m: A compass points to the magnetic, not the geographic, North Pole.

112922.q: Why does the magnetic declination at a place change over the years?
a: Because the Earth's magnetic poles move
112922.e: The Earth's magnetic field is constantly changing, and the magnetic poles shift. That is why accurate maps state which year the declination shown applies to.
112922.m: Because the magnetic poles move, declination changes over time.

112923.q: Roughly how big is the magnetic declination in Switzerland today (as of 2025)?
112923.e: In Switzerland the compass needle today points only about 2 to 4 degrees east of geographic north. For hikes this small difference usually hardly matters.
112923.m: In Switzerland the declination is small today.

112924.q: In Switzerland the magnetic declination is small today. What does this mean for a hike with a compass?
a: The needle points almost exactly to map north
112924.e: Because the difference is only a few degrees, the needle points almost in the north direction of the map. For short hikes that is usually enough.
112924.m: With small declination, the compass points almost to map north.

112925.q: Who has to take magnetic declination into account especially carefully?
112925.e: Over long distances even a small error in angle leads to a big miss of the target. So navigators include the declination in their courses.
112925.m: Anyone navigating by compass must allow for declination.

112926.q: Why can a compass give a wrong reading next to a large piece of iron?
a: The iron makes the needle heavier
112926.e: Iron affects the magnetic field close to it. That is why the compass needle is deflected, for example in ships or cars.
112926.m: Iron nearby deflects the compass needle.

112927.q: What happens to the magnetic declination when you get very close to a magnetic pole?
a: It turns into a temperature reading
112927.e: Near the magnetic poles, the magnetic and geographic poles lie in very different directions. The declination there can be many dozens of degrees.
112927.m: Near the poles the declination can become huge.

112928.q: Which three metals are ferromagnetic at room temperature?
112928.e: Iron, nickel and cobalt are strongly attracted by magnets and can be magnetised. Most other metals, on the other hand, are hardly magnetic.
112928.m: Iron, nickel and cobalt are the classic ferromagnetic metals.

112929.q: What are the small regions in a ferromagnetic material that act like tiny magnets called?
112929.e: Weiss domains, named after the physicist Pierre-Ernest Weiss, are evenly magnetised regions. In an unmagnetised piece of iron they point in all directions.
112929.m: Magnetic domains are the tiny elementary magnets in iron.

112930.q: What happens to the magnetic domains when you magnetise a piece of iron?
a: They line up in a common direction
They move out of the iron
112930.e: An external magnetic field turns the magnetisation of the domains in one direction. Their effects add up, and the iron becomes magnetic itself.
112930.m: When iron is magnetised, its domains line up.

112931.q: What happens to a permanent magnet if you heat it very strongly?
112931.e: Strong heat jumbles up the tiny elementary magnets inside. For iron this happens from around 770 degrees Celsius.

112932.q: Which famous pair of scientists studied magnetism and radioactivity?
112932.e: Pierre Curie studied how magnets react to heat. With his wife Marie Curie he discovered new radioactive substances.
112932.m: Pierre and Marie Curie were a famous pair of scientists.

112933.q: What materials are the strongest permanent magnets available today made of?
112933.e: Neodymium-iron-boron magnets are the strongest permanent magnets. They are found in headphones, electric motors and wind turbines.
112933.m: Neodymium magnets are the strongest permanent magnets.

112934.q: Does a magnet attract every kind of steel equally strongly?
a: No, many stainless steels hardly at all
Yes, every steel sticks equally strongly
Yes, but only in the cold
112934.e: Many stainless steels, for example in sinks, contain chromium and nickel. Although they contain a lot of iron, a magnet hardly sticks to them.

112935.q: Which material is suitable as the core of an electromagnet that should lose its force as soon as it is switched off?
112935.e: Soft iron becomes strongly magnetic in an electromagnet. When you switch off the current, it loses its magnetism almost completely.
112935.m: Soft iron is a good core for electromagnets.

112936.q: Why does an electromagnet usually have a soft iron core?
a: It strengthens the magnetic field and loses it again when switched off
112936.e: The iron core concentrates and strengthens the coil's magnetic field many times over. Soft iron keeps hardly any magnetism after switching off, so the magnet really lets go.
112936.m: A soft iron core makes an electromagnet strong and switchable.

112937.q: What happens to the poles of an electromagnet when you reverse the direction of the current?
a: The north and south poles swap places
The magnet becomes twice as strong
Nothing, the poles stay the same
112937.e: The direction of the magnetic field depends on the direction of the current. If the current is reversed, the magnetic poles swap too.
112937.m: Reversing the current reverses the poles of an electromagnet.

112938.q: What are large electromagnets used for in scrapyards?
a: To lift scrap iron and drop it again
112938.e: A lifting magnet holds iron parts as long as current flows. When it is switched off, the scrap falls down in the right place.
112938.m: An electromagnet can pick up loads and let go at the press of a button.

112939.q: What are huge electromagnets needed for in the particle accelerator at CERN near Geneva?
a: To steer the particle beams on their path
To pump water out of the tunnel
To warm the air in the tunnel
112939.e: Fast charged particles are deflected by magnetic fields. In the Large Hadron Collider, thousands of powerful electromagnets force them onto their ring-shaped path.
112939.m: At CERN, huge electromagnets steer the particle beams.

112940.q: What do you need to build a simple electromagnet yourself?
a: An iron nail, wire and a battery
A wooden stick, string and a candle
112940.e: You wind insulated wire around an iron nail and connect the ends to a battery. As long as current flows, the nail attracts paper clips.
112940.m: Wire, an iron nail and a battery make an electromagnet.

112941.q: What effect does a larger current have on an electromagnet?
112941.e: The strength of a coil's magnetic field grows with the current. Without the iron becoming saturated, double the current means roughly a field twice as strong.
112941.m: More current makes an electromagnet stronger.

112942.q: Which household device uses an electromagnet to unlock a door at the press of a button?
112942.e: In an electric door opener, an electromagnet pulls back a bolt as soon as someone presses the button. Then the front door can be pushed open.
112942.m: An electric door opener works with an electromagnet.

112943.q: What happens to an electromagnet without an iron core when you switch off the current?
a: Its magnetic field disappears at once
112943.e: Without current there are no more moving charges to produce a magnetic field. That is why the field of a plain wire coil disappears at once.
112943.m: Without current, a wire coil has no magnetic field.

112944.q: Why is the copper wire of a coil coated with varnish?
a: So that the turns are insulated from each other
So that it shines more nicely
112944.e: Without insulation the current would jump from turn to turn instead of flowing through the whole wire. The thin varnish prevents this short circuit.
112944.m: The varnish insulates the turns of a coil from each other.

112945.q: How does the magnetic field of a coil change if, with the same current and length, you increase the number of turns from 200 to 400?
a: It becomes four times as strong
112945.e: The field strength inside a long coil is proportional to the number of turns. 400 is double 200, so the field doubles.
112945.m: Double the number of turns means a coil field twice as strong.

112946.q: From the outside, which magnet does the magnetic field of a current-carrying coil resemble?
a: A ring magnet with no poles
112946.e: Like a bar magnet, a coil has a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other. Outside, the field lines run in similar arcs.
112946.m: A current-carrying coil acts like a bar magnet from the outside.

112947.q: What is the magnetic field like inside a long coil?
112947.e: Inside a long coil the field lines run parallel and equally dense. The field is almost equally strong everywhere there.
112947.m: Inside a long coil the field is almost uniform.

112948.q: What can you use to greatly increase the magnetic field of a current-carrying coil?
112948.e: An iron core inside the coil strengthens the magnetic field very much. This makes a powerful electromagnet.
112948.m: An iron core strengthens a coil's magnetic field.

112949.q: What is a coil without an iron core called?
112949.e: In an air-core coil there is only air or a non-magnetic former inside. Its magnetic field is weaker than with an iron core, but it is well suited to very fast alternating currents, for example in radios.
112949.m: A coil without an iron core is called an air-core coil.

112950.q: What happens to a piece of iron next to a coil as soon as current flows through the coil?
112950.e: When current flows through the coil, a magnetic field forms. This attracts iron; this is how electric door openers work, for example.
112950.m: A coil with current attracts iron.

112951.q: A coil has 25 layers with 40 turns each. How many turns does it have altogether?
112951.e: You multiply the number of layers by the turns per layer, so 25 times 40. That makes 1000 turns.
112951.m: Layers times turns per layer gives the total number of turns.

112952.q: Which country did the physicist Hans Christian Ørsted come from?
112952.e: Ørsted was a Danish physicist and chemist and taught at the University of Copenhagen. There he made his famous discovery about electromagnetism.
112952.m: Hans Christian Ørsted was a Danish scientist.

112953.q: What did Hans Christian Ørsted show in 1820?
a: Electric current produces a magnetic field
112953.e: Ørsted saw that a compass needle next to a wire swings as soon as current flows. So the current produces a magnetic field.
112953.m: Ørsted discovered that current produces a magnetic field.

112954.q: How does a compass needle line up under a straight wire when a strong current flows?
112954.e: The magnetic field of the current acts on the needle across the direction of the wire. So the needle lines up across the wire, as long as the current's field is stronger than the Earth's magnetic field.
112954.m: Under a current-carrying wire, the compass needle turns across it.

112955.q: What did Ørsted observe when he reversed the direction of the current in the wire?
a: The needle swung the opposite way
112955.e: If you reverse the current, the direction of the magnetic field reverses too. The compass needle therefore turns to the other side.
112955.m: When the current is reversed, the needle's deflection reverses too.

112956.q: Which field of physics did Ørsted found with his discovery?
112956.e: Before Ørsted, electricity and magnetism were seen as separate things. His discovery was the starting point for the study of electromagnetism.
112956.m: The study of electromagnetism began with Ørsted.

112957.q: Which device showed Ørsted, in his famous discovery, that current has a magnetic effect?
112957.e: Ørsted held a wire over a compass needle. When current flowed, the needle turned.
112957.m: A compass needle revealed the current's magnetic field to Ørsted.

112958.q: In which city did Hans Christian Ørsted teach as a professor?
112958.e: Ørsted taught at the University of Copenhagen, the capital of Denmark. That is also where he made his famous discovery.
112958.m: Ørsted did his research in Copenhagen.

112959.q: What forms around a wire through which current flows?
112959.e: Every current produces a magnetic field around the wire. Ørsted was the first to observe this in 1820.
112959.m: Wherever current flows, a magnetic field forms.

112960.q: Why does the hammer of an electric bell keep striking the bell as long as you press the button?
a: The current is constantly broken and switched on again
The battery is recharged again and again
The hammer is moved by the wind
The bell attracts the hammer magnetically
112960.e: When the electromagnet pulls the hammer, a contact opens and the current stops. A spring pulls the armature back, the contact closes, and everything starts again.
112960.m: In a bell, the current is broken again and again.

112961.q: Which part of an electric bell pulls the hammer?
112961.e: When current flows, the electromagnet becomes magnetic and pulls the iron armature with the hammer. The hammer then strikes the bell.
112961.m: The electromagnet pulls the hammer of the bell.

112962.q: What pulls the armature of an electric bell back after each strike?
a: A rubber band on the bell
112962.e: As soon as the circuit is broken, the electromagnet loses its force. A leaf spring pulls the armature back and closes the contact again.
112962.m: A spring returns the armature of the bell to its starting position.

112963.q: Which energy conversion takes place in an electric bell?
a: Electrical energy becomes movement and sound
112963.e: Via the electromagnet, the current sets the hammer moving. Striking the bell produces the sound, and some of the energy is lost as heat.
112963.m: A bell turns electrical energy into movement and sound.

112964.q: What is the switch you use to ring a doorbell at the front door called?
112964.e: A push button only closes the circuit as long as you press it. When you let go, it opens again.
112964.m: A bell is rung with a push button.

112965.q: What is a bell transformer for in a household installation?
a: It lowers the mains voltage to a safe extra-low voltage
112965.e: Bell systems work with an extra-low voltage of a few volts. The bell transformer reduces the 230 volts from the mains accordingly.
112965.m: A bell transformer supplies a safe low voltage.

112966.q: What often appears at the contact breaker of an electric bell when the contact opens?
112966.e: When the contact opens, the coil tries to keep the current going. As a result a small spark often jumps across, which wears the contacts over time.
112966.m: Small sparks often jump at the contacts of a bell.

112967.q: How does an electric chime with a ding-dong sound make its sound differently from a bell?
a: An iron rod strikes each of two tone bars once
A hammer strikes a bell non-stop
Air is blown into a whistle
112967.e: In a chime, a coil pulls an iron rod that strikes one tone bar; when released, it springs against the second. This makes the double tone instead of continuous ringing.
112967.m: A chime strikes only once when you press and once when you let go.

a: To switch a big circuit with a small current
112968.e: In a relay, a small control current pulls an armature via an electromagnet. This closes or opens contacts in a second, often much stronger circuit.
112968.m: A relay switches a big circuit with a small current.

112969.q: Which part moves the switching contacts in an electromechanical relay?
a: An armature pulled by the electromagnet
112969.e: When current flows through the relay coil, the iron armature is pulled. In doing so it pushes the contacts together or apart.
112969.m: The armature in a relay moves the contacts.

112970.q: What is a relay contact called that closes when current flows through the coil?
112970.e: A normally open contact is open at rest and closes when the relay pulls in. A normally closed contact does exactly the opposite.
112970.m: A normally open contact closes when the relay pulls in.

112971.q: What typical noise does an electromechanical relay make when it switches?
112971.e: When pulling in and letting go, the armature audibly hits the core or the stop. The clicking of the indicator in older cars often comes from a relay.
112971.m: A relay clicks when it switches.

112972.q: What switching elements was Konrad Zuse's Z3 computer mainly made of?
112972.e: In 1941 Konrad Zuse built his program-controlled Z3 computer from around 2000 telephone relays. Valves and transistors only took over later.
112972.m: The early Z3 computer calculated with relays.

112973.q: In which technology did relays first become important in the 19th century for boosting signals over long distances?
112973.e: On long telegraph lines the signal grew weak. A relay used it to switch a new, fresh circuit and passed the signal on.
112973.m: Relays made long-distance telegraph lines possible.

112974.q: What safety advantage does a relay offer between the control circuit and the load circuit?
a: The two circuits are electrically separated
It makes the load current harmless
It prevents any use of electricity
112974.e: In a relay the control and load circuits are only linked by the magnetic field. So you can switch mains voltage with a safe low voltage.
112974.m: A relay separates the control and load circuits electrically.

112975.q: What advantage does a solid-state relay have over a mechanical relay?
a: It switches silently and hardly wears out
It needs no current at all
It can only switch very small currents
112975.e: Solid-state relays switch electronically, without moving parts. So they don't click and their contacts don't wear out.
112975.m: Solid-state relays switch without moving parts.

112976.q: Which part of a loudspeaker makes the air vibrate?
112976.e: The cone moves back and forth, squeezing and thinning the air. This creates sound waves.
112976.m: The cone of a loudspeaker produces the sound waves.

112977.q: What is the coil attached to the cone in a dynamic loudspeaker called?
112977.e: The voice coil is firmly attached to the cone. When the changing sound signal flows through it, it is pushed back and forth, and the cone with it.
112977.m: The voice coil moves the loudspeaker cone.

112978.q: What sits next to the voice coil in a dynamic loudspeaker?
112978.e: The permanent magnet produces a fixed magnetic field. Only together with the magnetic field of the current-carrying voice coil is movement produced.
112978.m: In a loudspeaker, the voice coil works together with a permanent magnet.

112979.q: What is a loudspeaker called that mainly reproduces low notes?
112979.e: Woofers have large cones because a lot of air has to be moved for low notes. Tweeters, on the other hand, are small and light.
112979.m: Low notes come from the woofer with its large cone.

112980.q: Why does a speaker box often have one large and one small loudspeaker?
a: The large one plays low notes, the small one high notes
The small one is just a spare part
The large one is just for decoration
112980.e: For low notes a lot of air has to be moved, which needs a large cone. A small, light loudspeaker reproduces high notes better.
112980.m: Large loudspeakers play low notes, small ones high notes.

112981.q: Which device works on the same principle as a dynamic loudspeaker, only the other way round?
112981.e: In a dynamic microphone, sound moves a diaphragm with a coil in a magnetic field. This produces an electrical voltage that represents the sound signal.
112981.m: A dynamic microphone is a loudspeaker in reverse.

112982.q: Why does a loudspeaker cone move back and forth and not just in one direction?
a: The sound signal is an alternating current that keeps changing direction
The cone is connected to clockwork
The permanent magnet keeps switching off
The air randomly pushes the cone back
112982.e: The sound signal keeps changing direction, exactly in time with the sound. As a result the voice coil is alternately attracted and repelled.
112982.m: Alternating current makes the loudspeaker cone vibrate.

112983.q: Which devices contain very small loudspeakers right at the ear?
112983.e: Headphones contain small transducers that work on the same principle. Because they are right at the ear, they need only a little power.
112983.m: Headphones are tiny loudspeakers at the ear.

112984.q: Why does a maglev train have no rolling resistance while it is moving?
a: It floats above the track without touching it
112984.e: Magnetic forces lift the vehicle and guide it sideways. Because there are no wheels and rails, there is no rolling friction between vehicle and track.
112984.m: A maglev train floats above the track without touching it.

112985.q: What was the maglev train developed in Germany called?
112985.e: The Transrapid was developed in Germany over decades and tested on a test track in Emsland. No commercial line was ever built in Germany.
112985.m: The Transrapid is the German maglev train.

112986.q: In which city does a Transrapid line run to the airport in regular service?
112986.e: In Shanghai a Transrapid line has linked the city with Pudong airport since 2003. The train used to run at over 430 km/h, since 2021 at most 300 km/h (as of 2025).
112986.m: In Shanghai the Transrapid runs to the airport.

112987.q: Which country set the speed record for rail vehicles of over 600 km/h with a maglev train in 2015?
112987.e: In 2015 the Japanese SCMaglev reached 603 km/h on a test track. That is the record for rail vehicles carrying people.
112987.m: Japan's maglev holds the speed record at 603 km/h.

112988.q: What drive moves a maglev train forwards?
112988.e: A linear motor is like an electric motor that has been cut open and rolled out flat. A travelling magnetic field in the track pulls the vehicle forwards.
112988.m: Maglev trains are driven by linear motors.

112989.q: What was the Swiss project for an underground maglev train in tubes with little air called?
112989.e: Swissmetro planned maglev trains in tunnel tubes with very thin air between Swiss cities. The project was never carried out.
112989.m: Swissmetro was a Swiss maglev project that was never built.

112990.q: What advantage does a maglev train have over a wheel-on-rail train?
a: Less wear, because the vehicle and track don't touch
It needs no energy at all
It can drive on any normal road
It flies through the air without a track
112990.e: Because nothing rubs together, the track and vehicle hardly wear out. On the other hand it needs its own expensive track.
112990.m: Without contact, a maglev train hardly wears out.

112991.q: Roughly how big is the gap in which the Transrapid floats above its track?
112991.e: The Transrapid floats only about one centimetre above its stator packs. Electronic controls constantly keep this small gap the same.
112991.m: The Transrapid floats only about one centimetre high.

112992.q: Which force keeps the Transrapid floating?
a: The attraction between electromagnets and the track
112992.e: Electromagnets reach under the track from below and are pulled up towards it. This lifts the train.
112992.m: The Transrapid floats by magnetic attraction to the underside of the track.

112993.q: A steel knitting needle is stroked several times with a magnet. What happens?
112993.e: When stroked, the elementary magnets in the steel line up. Part of this magnetism remains afterwards.

112994.q: In which century did Ørsted discover the link between electric current and magnetism?
112994.e: Ørsted made his discovery in 1820. That belongs to the 19th century.
112994.m: Ørsted discovered electromagnetism in the 19th century.

112995.q: Why are loudspeakers built into a box?
a: So that the low notes sound powerful
So that the loudspeaker doesn't rust
So that the magnet becomes stronger
112995.e: The cone pushes the air away at the front and sucks it in at the back. Without a box this evens out around the edge, and the low notes in particular become weak.
112995.m: Loudspeakers only have powerful bass in a box.

112996.q: Around which day does St John's wort start to flower, the day it is named after?
112996.e: St John's wort flowers from about the end of June. Its name recalls St John's Day on 24 June, the feast day of John the Baptist.
112996.m: St John's wort is named after St John's Day in June.

112997.q: What colour are the flowers of St John's wort?
112997.e: St John's wort has bright yellow flowers with five petals. You find it in summer on roadsides and in dry meadows.
112997.m: St John's wort has yellow flowers in summer.

112998.q: What do you see when you hold a leaf of St John's wort up to the light?
112998.e: The leaves contain tiny oil glands that look like little holes against the light. That is why the species is called “perforatum” in Latin, meaning full of holes.
112998.m: Against the light, St John's wort leaves look as if they are full of holes.

112999.q: What colour does oil turn if you soak St John's wort flowers in it?
112999.e: The pigment hypericin from the flowers turns the oil deep red. This so-called red oil is traditionally used for skin care.
112999.m: St John's wort oil turns red because of the pigment hypericin.

113000.q: What are St John's wort preparations mainly used for in herbal medicine?
113000.e: Studies show that St John's wort extract can help with mild to moderate depressed moods. The effect only begins after a few weeks.
113000.m: St John's wort is used for mildly low mood.

113001.q: Which side effect can St John's wort have on the skin?
a: It becomes more sensitive to sunlight
113001.e: Substances in St John's wort can make the skin more sensitive to light. Anyone taking it should avoid strong sun.
113001.m: St John's wort can make the skin more sensitive to sunlight.

113002.q: Why should you not simply take St John's wort together with other medicines?
113002.e: St John's wort speeds up the breakdown of many other medicines in the liver. This can make them work less well, so you should ask an expert first.
113002.m: St John's wort can weaken the effect of other medicines.

113003.q: What is typical of the stem of St John's wort?
a: It has two fine ridges running along it
113003.e: The stem of St John's wort is round but has two raised ridges along its length. This lets you tell it apart from similar St John's wort species.
113003.m: The stem of St John's wort has two fine ridges.

113004.q: What shape are the leaves of ribwort plantain?
a: Long and narrow like a lance
113004.e: Ribwort plantain has long, narrow, pointed leaves. Its Latin name “lanceolata” means lance-shaped.
113004.m: Ribwort plantain has long, narrow leaves.

113005.q: How do the leaf veins of ribwort plantain run?
a: In a star shape from the centre
113005.e: In ribwort plantain, several strong veins run almost parallel from the base to the tip. If you tear a leaf, you can clearly see these fibres.
113005.m: The leaf veins of ribwort plantain run almost parallel.

113006.q: What is ribwort plantain traditionally used against as a syrup or tea?
113006.e: As a tea or syrup, ribwort plantain coats the irritated throat and protects it. That is why it is a well-known home remedy for coughs.
113006.m: Ribwort plantain is a well-known home remedy for coughs.

113007.q: What can you do with a crushed ribwort plantain leaf when you are out and about?
a: Put it on a mosquito bite
Stick it on like a plaster
113007.e: The juice of a crushed leaf cools and soothes itching after mosquito bites or nettle stings. That is why ribwort plantain is known as the meadow's plaster.
113007.m: A crushed ribwort plantain leaf soothes itchy bites.

113008.q: Which substances in ribwort plantain coat irritated mucous membranes and soothe them?
113008.e: Mucilage swells up with water and forms a protective film. This calms the urge to cough in the throat.
113008.m: Mucilage in ribwort plantain soothes irritated mucous membranes.

113009.q: Where does ribwort plantain grow especially often in Switzerland?
a: Only high in the mountains above 3,000 metres
113009.e: Ribwort plantain is very common and grows in meadows, pastures and on roadsides. It also copes well with being trodden on.
113009.m: Ribwort plantain often grows in meadows and by paths.

113010.q: What does the flower head of ribwort plantain look like?
a: A brownish spike on a long stalk
A yellow head like a dandelion
113010.e: The tiny flowers sit tightly packed in a brownish spike on a long, leafless stalk. The pale stamens stick out like a ring.
113010.m: Ribwort plantain flowers in a brown spike on a long stalk.

113011.q: What is a close relative of ribwort plantain with broad, roundish leaves called?
113011.e: Broadleaf plantain belongs to the same genus as ribwort plantain. It often grows right on trodden paths.
113011.m: Broadleaf plantain is a relative of ribwort plantain.

113012.q: What colour are the flowers of the pot marigold usually?
113012.e: The pot marigold shines in strong orange or yellow. It is often planted in gardens.
113012.m: The pot marigold flowers orange or yellow.

113013.q: How long does a garden pot marigold normally live?
113013.e: The garden pot marigold is usually an annual. But it often seeds itself, so new plants grow the next year.
113013.m: The pot marigold is usually an annual and seeds itself.

113014.q: Where does the German name of the pot marigold, “Ringelblume” (ring flower), come from?
a: From a ring around the root
113014.e: The fruits of the pot marigold are strongly curled, almost like little rings. That is where its German name comes from.
113014.m: The German name Ringelblume comes from its curled-up seeds.

113015.q: Which plant family does the pot marigold belong to?
113015.e: Like the daisy and the sunflower, the pot marigold belongs to the daisy family. What looks like one flower is a head made of many small single flowers.
113015.m: The pot marigold belongs to the daisy family.

113016.q: What were pot marigold flowers used for in cooking in the past?
113016.e: The petals colour food yellow and were therefore used as a cheap substitute for expensive saffron. They are edible.
113016.m: Pot marigold flowers were used as a cheap saffron substitute for colouring.

113017.q: What do many pot marigolds do when it rains or in the evening?
113017.e: The flower heads of the pot marigold close in dull weather and at night. That is why it used to be seen as a weather forecaster.
113017.m: The pot marigold closes its flowers in rain and in the evening.

113018.q: What is the pot marigold often used for today?
a: As animal feed in the zoo
113018.e: Ointments that help with small wounds and rough skin are made from pot marigolds. In the past it was used in pharmacies.
113018.m: Marigold ointment cares for the skin.

113019.q: Until when do pot marigolds often flower in the garden?
a: Until the first frost in autumn
Only for one single week in May
113019.e: The pot marigold flowers for a very long time, from early summer into autumn. Only the frost brings it to an end.
113019.m: Pot marigolds often flower until the first frost.

113020.q: What is valerian mainly used for in herbal medicine?
a: To calm down and for trouble falling asleep
To wake up in the morning
113020.e: Valerian is considered a mild calming remedy. It is used for nervousness and trouble falling asleep as a tea, drops or tablets.
113020.m: Valerian has a calming effect and helps you fall asleep.

113021.q: Which part of valerian is used as a remedy?
113021.e: The active substances are mainly in the rootstock and the roots. These are dug up, dried and processed.
113021.m: With valerian, the root is used.

113022.q: Which pet is especially attracted by the smell of valerian?
113022.e: Many cats react very excitedly to the smell of valerian, rolling around and purring. That is why there are cat toys with valerian.
113022.m: Many cats love the smell of valerian.

113023.q: What do most people think of the smell of dried valerian root?
113023.e: When it dries, isovaleric acid is formed, among other things. It has a strong smell that reminds people of sweaty feet.
113023.m: Dried valerian root has a strong, unpleasant smell.

113024.q: What colour are the flowers of common valerian?
113024.e: Common valerian has lots of small white to pale pink flowers in umbrella-like clusters. They have a sweetish scent.
113024.m: Common valerian flowers white to pale pink.

113025.q: Where does common valerian like to grow in nature?
a: In damp places such as stream banks
On tree bark as an air plant
113025.e: Valerian loves damp soil. You find it on the banks of streams and ditches, in damp meadows and floodplain forests.
113025.m: Valerian likes to grow in damp places.

113026.q: How tall can common valerian grow?
113026.e: Common valerian is a tall perennial. It usually grows between half a metre and one and a half metres tall, sometimes even a bit taller.
113026.m: Common valerian can grow more than a metre tall.

113027.q: Which pet reacts especially strongly to the smell of valerian?
113027.e: Many cats are attracted by the scent of valerian root. They rub against it and roll on the ground.
113027.m: Cats love the smell of valerian.

113028.q: What is fennel tea traditionally drunk for especially often?
113028.e: The essential oils in fennel relax the gut and help against wind. That is why fennel tea is a well-known tummy tea.
113028.m: Fennel tea helps with tummy ache and wind.

113029.e: Fennel is a sturdy perennial and usually grows between half a metre and two metres tall. Its stems are finely grooved.
113029.m: Fennel can grow up to about two metres tall.

113030.q: Which kitchen herb are fennel leaves often confused with because of their fine leaves?
113030.e: Dill and fennel both have hair-fine, divided leaves and are closely related members of the carrot family. You can easily tell them apart by their taste.
113030.m: Fennel leaves look very similar to dill.

113031.q: Which butterfly likes to lay its eggs on fennel, dill and carrot?
113031.e: Swallowtail caterpillars feed on members of the carrot family such as fennel, dill, carrot and wild carrot. In the garden you sometimes find the green, black and orange striped caterpillars right on the fennel.
113031.m: The swallowtail caterpillar likes eating fennel.

113032.q: Which part of Florence fennel is eaten as a vegetable?
a: The thickened leaf bases that form a bulb
113032.e: In Florence fennel, the thick leaf stalks wrap around each other at the bottom to form a bulb. This is eaten raw in salad or cooked.
113032.m: With Florence fennel, you eat the bulb made of thickened leaf bases.

113033.q: Botanically speaking, what are so-called fennel seeds?
113033.e: What you buy as fennel seeds are really small split fruits. Each one contains a seed.
113033.m: Botanically, fennel seeds are small fruits.

113034.q: Which region does fennel originally come from?
113034.e: Wild fennel grows on the coasts of the Mediterranean. The Romans and Greeks already used it as a spice and medicinal plant.

113035.q: What do fennel leaves look like?
113035.e: Fennel leaves are divided into many hair-fine tips. They are also used as a kitchen herb.
113035.m: Fennel leaves are fine and thread-like.

113036.q: What does the underside of silverweed leaves look like?
113036.e: The feathery leaves are thickly covered with silvery hairs underneath. That is why the plant is called silverweed.
113036.m: Silverweed has silvery undersides to its leaves.

113037.q: Where does the first part of the German name of silverweed, “Gänsefingerkraut” (goose finger herb), come from?
a: It likes to grow on goose pastures
It only grows on geese's necks
113037.e: The plant is common on pastures and by village ponds, where geese used to be kept. Geese like eating it.
113037.m: Silverweed likes to grow where geese graze.

113038.e: Silverweed has single yellow flowers with five petals. They sit on long stalks.

113039.q: Which plant family does silverweed belong to?
113039.e: Silverweed is closely related to the cinquefoils. Like the rose, apple and strawberry, these belong to the rose family.
113039.m: Silverweed belongs to the rose family.

113040.q: How does silverweed spread across the ground?
a: With seeds that fly like parachutes
It does not, it stays on its own
113040.e: Silverweed forms runners above ground that put down roots. This creates whole carpets of plants, similar to strawberries.

113041.q: What is silverweed traditionally used against?
113041.e: In folk medicine, silverweed is said to relieve cramps. People drink it as a tea for stomach cramps.
113041.m: Silverweed is traditionally used against stomach cramps.

113042.q: Which substances make silverweed tea helpful for mild diarrhoea?
113042.e: Tannins slightly tighten the mucous membranes. This can help with mild diarrhoea.
113042.m: Tannins in silverweed help with mild diarrhoea.

113043.e: Each leaf is made of many small, toothed leaflets. They sit in pairs on a shared stalk.

113044.q: What does willow bark tea taste like?
113044.e: Willow bark contains tannins and bitter substances. So the tea tastes bitter and makes your mouth pucker a little.
113044.m: Willow bark tea tastes bitter and harsh.

113045.q: Where does the name of the active substance salicin come from?
a: From the Latin name of the willow, Salix
113045.e: Willows form the genus Salix. The names salicin and salicylic acid come from this.
113045.m: Salicin is named after the willow, Salix in Latin.

113046.q: Who should not take willow bark because of an intolerance?
113046.e: Willow bark contains substances called salicylates, similar to those in the painkiller aspirin. People who are oversensitive to these should avoid it.
113046.m: If you cannot tolerate aspirin, do not take willow bark either.

113047.q: Which well-known painkiller was developed by copying the active substances in willow bark?
113047.e: Acetylsalicylic acid was later developed from the willow substance salicin. It went on sale as aspirin at the end of the 19th century.
113047.m: Aspirin was developed by copying willow bark.

113048.q: Which complaints is willow bark often used for in herbal medicine today?
a: For mild back and joint pain
113048.e: Herbal medicines with willow bark are used mainly for mild back pain and rheumatic complaints. They are weaker than modern painkillers.
113048.m: Today willow bark is often used for mild back and joint pain.

113049.q: According to the European Medicines Agency, who are medicines made from willow bark not recommended for?
113049.e: As with aspirin, there is not enough safety data for children and teenagers. That is why the European Medicines Agency advises against it for under-18s.
113049.m: Willow bark is not recommended for children and teenagers.

113050.q: Why does willow bark tea work more slowly than an aspirin tablet?
a: The body first has to convert the salicin
Tea is not absorbed by the body
Willow bark contains no active substance at all
Hot water destroys all active substances at once
113050.e: Salicin is a precursor. Only in the gut and liver is it turned into the active salicylic acid, and that takes time.
113050.m: The salicin from willow bark first has to be converted in the body.

113051.q: Which part of the willow is used for the remedy?
113051.e: The bark is peeled from young twigs, two to three years old, in spring. That is where the content of the active substance is high.
113051.m: Willow bark tea is made from the bark of young twigs.

113052.q: The name aspirin contains the syllable “spir”. Which plant does it come from?
113052.e: Salicylic acid used to be obtained from meadowsweet, which was then called Spiraea. The “A” stands for acetyl and “spir” for Spiraea.
113052.m: The name aspirin contains Spiraea, the old name for meadowsweet.

113053.q: Which organ do the active substances in foxglove affect?
113053.e: The active substances in foxglove make the heart muscle beat more strongly. But in too large an amount they are deadly.
113053.m: Foxglove contains substances that act on the heart.

113054.q: What do the flowers of the common foxglove look like?
a: Like bells on a tall flower spike
Like flat stars on the ground
113054.e: The common foxglove forms a tall flower spike with many hanging, tube-shaped bells. Inside they are often spotted with dark marks.
113054.m: The common foxglove has bell-shaped flowers on a tall stem.

113057.q: Where does the common foxglove especially like to grow in nature?
a: In forest clearings with acid soil
In salt water on the beach
On glaciers in the eternal ice
113057.e: The common foxglove likes bright spots in the forest, such as clearings and areas where trees have been felled. It prefers acid soils low in lime.
113057.m: The common foxglove likes to grow in forest clearings.

113058.q: Which harmless plant are foxglove leaves sometimes dangerously confused with before the plant flowers?
113058.e: Before it flowers, foxglove forms only a rosette of hairy leaves. These look like comfrey leaves, which has already led to poisonings.
113058.m: Foxglove leaves can be confused with comfrey.

113059.q: What colour are the flowers of the large yellow foxglove and the small yellow foxglove, which grow wild in Switzerland?
113059.e: The large yellow foxglove and the small yellow foxglove have pale yellow flowers and grow in Swiss forests and at forest edges. Like the common foxglove, they are poisonous.
113059.m: Yellow-flowered kinds of foxglove grow wild in Switzerland.

113060.q: Why must people never make foxglove into tea themselves?
a: The healing amount and the poisonous amount are very close together
It does not dissolve in water
113060.e: With foxglove's active substances, the gap between an effective dose and a poisonous dose is very small. That is why they are only prescribed as medicines in exact doses.
113060.m: With foxglove, the difference between medicine and poison is very small.

113061.e: Sebastian Kneipp was a Catholic priest. As the priest of a Bavarian village, he treated many people with water treatments.
113061.m: Sebastian Kneipp was a Catholic priest.

113062.q: Which element is the Kneipp cure especially linked with?
113062.e: Kneipp relied on showers, wraps and baths with cold water. They are meant to strengthen the circulation and the body's defences.
113062.m: The Kneipp cure relies mainly on cold water.

113063.q: According to Sebastian Kneipp, what else besides water is part of a healthy life?
a: As much time in bed as possible
113063.e: Kneipp's teaching rests on five pillars: water, medicinal plants, exercise, diet and a balanced way of life. Together they are meant to strengthen the whole person.
113063.m: Kneipp's teaching also includes exercise and healthy food.

113064.q: Which treatment is typical of Kneipp facilities, which also exist in Switzerland?
a: Wading through water with a stork walk
113064.e: You walk through cold water about as deep as your calves, lifting your legs high like a stork. This is meant to boost blood flow.
113064.m: When water wading, you walk like a stork through cold water.

113065.q: In which century did Sebastian Kneipp live?
113065.e: Sebastian Kneipp lived from 1821 to 1897. His teaching became world-famous towards the end of the 19th century.
113065.m: Sebastian Kneipp lived in the 19th century.

113066.q: What made Sebastian Kneipp famous far beyond his village?
a: A book about his water cure
113066.e: In 1886 Kneipp's book “My Water Cure” was published. It was translated into many languages and made him world-famous.
113066.m: Kneipp became famous with his book about the water cure.

113067.q: According to his own account, how did the young Sebastian Kneipp cure himself of his serious lung disease?
a: With short baths in the cold Danube
With long trips to the seaside
113067.e: Kneipp fell ill with tuberculosis as a student. He bathed several times briefly in the ice-cold water of the Danube and believed this was why he got better.
113067.m: As a young man, Kneipp bathed in the cold Danube to get well.

113068.q: What do you do in a Kneipp spa town?
a: You recover with water treatments and exercise
113068.e: In Kneipp spa towns such as Bad Wörishofen, where Kneipp himself worked, there are wading pools, water showers and walking paths. Guests are meant to build up new strength.
113068.m: In Kneipp spa towns you recover with water and exercise.

113069.q: On which river is Bingen, which Hildegard is named after?
113069.e: Bingen lies on the Rhine in Germany, where the Nahe flows into the Rhine. Hildegard founded her convent nearby.

113070.q: Which cereal did Hildegard of Bingen value especially highly?
113070.e: Hildegard praised spelt as especially easy to digest. That is why spelt is still often linked with her today.
113070.m: Hildegard of Bingen especially valued spelt.

113071.q: Apart from religion, what did Hildegard of Bingen also write books about?
113071.e: In works such as the “Physica”, she described plants, animals and stones and how they are useful for health. Her writings are seen as early sources of natural history.
113071.m: Hildegard of Bingen wrote about nature and medicine.

113072.q: Which art was Hildegard of Bingen also active in?
a: She painted oil paintings on canvas
113072.e: Hildegard wrote many religious songs. Her music is still performed and recorded today.
113072.m: Hildegard of Bingen composed religious music.

a: A nun and abbess of a convent
113073.e: Hildegard lived in the 12th century and led a convent on the Rhine as its abbess. She wrote about faith, nature and medicine and composed music.
113073.m: Hildegard of Bingen was a nun and abbess.

113074.q: What did Hildegard of Bingen call the life force that makes all living things grow?
113074.e: Hildegard spoke of “viriditas”, the greening power. By this she meant the force of life and growth in plants, animals and people.
113074.m: Hildegard called nature's life force the greening power.

113075.q: What did Hildegard of Bingen write about in her work “Scivias”?
113075.e: Hildegard said she had had visions since childhood. In “Scivias”, which means “Know the Ways”, she wrote them down.

113076.q: In which present-day Swiss canton was Paracelsus born?
113076.e: Paracelsus was born around 1493 in Egg near Einsiedeln in the canton of Schwyz. His father was a doctor there.
113076.m: Paracelsus was born near Einsiedeln in the canton of Schwyz.

113077.q: Which science did Paracelsus want to use more in medicine by making remedies from minerals and metals?
113077.e: Paracelsus made remedies from substances such as mercury, sulphur or antimony. That is why he is seen as a pioneer of pharmaceutical chemistry.

113078.e: Paracelsus was a doctor, natural scientist and philosopher. He travelled all over Europe and worked, among other things, as the town doctor in Basel.
113078.m: Paracelsus was a doctor and natural scientist.

113079.q: In which language did Paracelsus unusually give his lectures in Basel?
113079.e: At that time scholars taught almost only in Latin. In Basel, Paracelsus spoke German so that more people could understand him.
113079.m: Paracelsus gave his lectures in German.

113080.q: What did Paracelsus want to express with his name?
a: That he surpassed the Roman doctor Celsus
That he was a pupil of Celsus
That he was born in Paracel
113080.e: “Para” means roughly “beyond”. The name is often taken to mean that he wanted to go beyond the famous Roman doctor Celsus.
113080.m: The name Paracelsus refers to the Roman doctor Celsus.

113081.q: What did Paracelsus publicly burn in Basel in 1527 to protest against the old medicine?
113081.e: Paracelsus threw a work by the doctor Avicenna into the Midsummer bonfire. He wanted to show that you should not just believe old books but observe for yourself.
113081.m: Paracelsus burnt an old medical book in Basel in protest.

113082.q: What does the doctrine of signatures, which Paracelsus supported, say?
a: The look of a plant shows what it heals
Plants should be labelled with names
Plants only work at full moon
113082.e: According to this old teaching, for example, a heart-shaped plant helps the heart. Science has not confirmed this idea.
113082.m: According to the doctrine of signatures, a plant's look shows its healing power.

113083.e: The Greek word “phyton” means plant. So phytotherapy is herbal medicine.

113084.q: In pharmacy, what is a dried plant part used as a remedy called?
113084.e: In pharmacy, a dried plant part such as camomile flowers or valerian root is called a crude drug. Here this has nothing to do with illegal drugs.
113084.m: In pharmacy, dried parts of medicinal plants are called crude drugs.

113085.q: What do you call a tea where you pour hot water over the herbs and leave them to steep?
113085.e: For an infusion, you pour boiling water over delicate plant parts such as flowers and leaves. Hard parts such as roots, on the other hand, are often boiled.
113085.m: For an infusion, you pour hot water over herbs.

113086.q: What is a plant extract made with alcohol called?
113086.e: For a tincture, plant parts are soaked in alcohol. This draws out the active substances and makes the extract keep for a long time.
113086.m: A tincture is a plant extract made with alcohol.

113087.q: Which substances give peppermint, camomile and fennel their strong scent?
113087.e: Essential oils evaporate easily and smell strong. Many of them relieve cramps or reduce inflammation.
113087.m: Essential oils give many medicinal plants their scent.

113088.q: Why should you only gather medicinal plants in nature if you can recognise them for certain?
a: Because you can confuse them with poisonous plants
Because all medicinal plants are banned
Because otherwise they wilt at once
Because they only work at night
113088.e: Some medicinal plants look very much like poisonous species. Confusing them can be dangerous.
113088.m: Only gather medicinal plants if you can recognise them for certain.

113089.q: What are healing methods such as herbal medicine, which add to conventional medicine, called?
113089.e: Complementary means adding to something. Phytotherapy is part of complementary medicine, which has been in the Federal Constitution since 2009.
113089.m: Phytotherapy is part of complementary medicine.

113090.q: Which tea made from a medicinal plant is often drunk for tummy ache?
113090.e: Camomile flowers have a calming and anti-inflammatory effect. Camomile tea is one of the best-known home remedies from herbal medicine.
113090.m: Camomile tea is a well-known home remedy for tummy ache.

113091.q: Which authority approves medicines in Switzerland, including those made from plants?
113091.e: Swissmedic is the Swiss authority that approves and supervises medicines. Herbal medicines also need approval.

113092.q: What typically happens to the resting pulse when someone does regular endurance training for months?
113092.e: A trained heart pumps more blood with each beat. So at rest it needs to beat less often.
113092.m: Regular endurance training lowers the resting pulse.

113093.q: What is the type of training called in which short, intense efforts alternate with recovery breaks?
113093.e: In interval training, hard sections are followed by planned breaks. This lets you run or ride very intensely several times.
113093.m: In interval training, effort and rest alternate.

113094.q: How long does the classic Cooper test last, in which you run as far as possible?
113094.e: The doctor Kenneth Cooper developed the test: you run as far as possible for 12 minutes. The distance shows your endurance.
113094.m: In the Cooper test, you run as far as possible in 12 minutes.

113095.q: What is the type of training called in which you run for a long time without a break at a steady, calm pace?
113095.e: With the continuous method, you keep moving for, say, 30 to 60 minutes without stopping. It mainly improves basic endurance.
113095.m: With the continuous method, you train for a long time without a break.

113096.q: During easy endurance training, what is a good sign that the pace is not too high?
113096.e: At a calm pace, your breath is still enough for whole sentences. This rule of thumb is often called “running without puffing”.
113096.m: If you can still chat during easy training, you are running at the right pace.

113097.q: Which of these sports mainly trains endurance?
113097.e: In cross-country skiing you move for a long time at a steady pace. Weightlifting, shot put and high jump are short bursts of strength.
113097.m: Cross-country skiing is a typical endurance sport.

113098.q: What is an enlarged, efficient heart resulting from endurance training called?
113098.e: With lots of endurance training, the heart muscle becomes bigger and stronger. In healthy athletes, this is a normal adaptation to training.
113098.m: A heart strengthened by training is called an athlete’s heart.

113099.q: Apart from the muscles, which body system is particularly strengthened by endurance training?
113099.e: Endurance needs a lot of oxygen in the muscles. That is why the heart, blood vessels and lungs in particular adapt.
113099.m: Endurance training strengthens the heart and circulation.

113100.q: What is the ability to repeat a force as often or as long as possible without getting tired called?
113100.e: You need strength endurance for rowing or doing lots of press-ups, for example. The muscles must produce force over a longer time.
113100.m: Strength endurance means being able to use strength for a long time.

113101.q: Which type of strength does a sprinter particularly need at the start to push off explosively?
113101.e: Explosive strength is the ability to develop a lot of force in a very short time. It is important for sprints and jumps.
113101.m: For explosive movements, you need explosive strength.

113102.q: What is the greatest force a muscle can produce in a single effort called?
113102.e: Maximum strength shows, for example, in the heaviest weight you can lift exactly once.
113102.m: Maximum strength is the highest possible force of a muscle.

113103.q: What is a group of several repetitions of a strength exercise, followed by a break, called?
113103.e: In strength training you might do 3 sets of 12 repetitions each. Between the sets, the muscle recovers briefly.
113103.m: Several repetitions in a row make up a set.

113104.q: What is an exercise called in which you hold your body still in one position, as in the plank?
113104.e: In a holding exercise, the muscles tense without the joints moving. The plank and the wall sit are typical examples.
113104.m: In the plank, the muscles hold the body still.

113105.q: Which exercise is strength training with your own body weight?
113105.e: In a press-up, you push up your own body weight. For dumbbell curls, leg presses and bench presses, you need weights or machines.
113105.m: Press-ups are strength training with your own body weight.

113106.q: Why should teenagers first learn strength exercises with little weight?
113106.e: Poor technique can overload the joints and back. With a light weight, you first learn the movement correctly.
113106.m: In strength exercises, clean technique comes before heavy weight.

113107.q: What is the ability to coordinate the movements of the arms and legs, as in star jumps, called?
