To find out your eye colour
Because otherwise the eyes dry out
114148.e: In REM sleep, when we dream a lot, the eyes move quickly back and forth. Electrodes next to the eyes record this.
114148.m: Rapid eye movements show dream sleep.

114149.q: What is measured in the sleep laboratory with electrodes on the chin and legs?
114149.e: Electrodes on the skin record the tension of the muscles. In REM sleep, muscle tension is very low.
114149.m: Electrodes on the chin and legs show how hard the muscles are working.

a: Breathing keeps stopping briefly during sleep
You grind your teeth at night
You suddenly fall asleep during the day
114150.e: In sleep apnoea, breathing keeps stopping briefly during sleep. People affected often snore loudly and are very tired during the day.
114150.m: In sleep apnoea, breathing stops during sleep.

114151.q: Which device is often used against sleep apnoea?
a: A breathing mask with slight positive pressure
114151.e: In CPAP therapy, a machine gently blows air into the airways through a mask. This keeps them open and the pauses in breathing disappear.
114151.m: A positive pressure mask keeps the airways open in sleep apnoea.

114152.q: What does a pulse oximeter on the finger measure during the night?
a: The oxygen saturation of the blood
114152.e: The pulse oximeter shines light through the finger and works out how much oxygen the blood is carrying. When breathing stops, this value falls.
114152.m: A pulse oximeter measures the oxygen in the blood.

114153.q: What happens in the illness narcolepsy?
a: You suddenly fall asleep during the day without wanting to
You cannot fall asleep at all at night
114153.e: People with narcolepsy have a disturbed control of sleeping and waking. They can fall asleep in the middle of everyday situations.
114153.m: With narcolepsy, sleep suddenly overwhelms you.

114154.q: Why did Switzerland introduce summer time?
a: To have the same time as its neighbouring countries
So that the cows would give more milk
114154.e: When the neighbouring countries had summer time and Switzerland did not, there were problems with train timetables and trade. That is why Switzerland has also had summer time since 1981.
114154.m: With summer time, Switzerland fell into line with its neighbours.

114155.q: What was Switzerland called in the summer of 1980 because it was the only country around without summer time?
114155.e: All the neighbouring countries had summer time in 1980, but Switzerland did not. This caused problems, for example with train timetables and trade.
114155.m: In 1980, Switzerland was a time island in Europe.

114156.q: On which day does summer time begin in Switzerland?
a: On the last Sunday in March
On the first Sunday in May
On the last Sunday in February
114156.e: On the last Sunday in March, the clock is put forward from 2 am to 3 am. Switzerland follows the EU rules on this.
114156.m: Summer time begins on the last Sunday in March.

114157.q: What happens to the length of your sleep on the night summer time begins?
a: The length of sleep stays the same
114157.e: The clock jumps from 2 am straight to 3 am. If you get up at the usual time, you have slept an hour less.
114157.m: In spring, the clock change costs you an hour of sleep.

114158.q: What is the standard time that applies in Switzerland in winter called?
114158.e: Central European Time (CET) is one hour ahead of universal time UTC. In summer, Central European Summer Time applies, two hours ahead.
114158.m: In winter, Central European Time applies in Switzerland.

114159.q: When was summer time first introduced in Europe?
114159.e: In 1916, in the middle of the First World War, Germany and Austria-Hungary introduced summer time. They wanted to save energy for lighting.
114159.m: Summer time has existed since the First World War.

114160.q: What was the original aim of summer time?
a: To make better use of daylight and save energy
To make the school holidays longer
114160.e: Putting the clock forward means it stays light for longer in the evening. This was supposed to mean less artificial light was needed. Today, however, the actual saving is disputed.
114160.m: Summer time was meant to help make better use of daylight.

114161.q: Which way do you turn the clock in spring when the clocks change?
114161.e: A well-known memory aid is “spring forward, fall back”. So in spring you put the clock forward, and in autumn you put it back.
114161.m: In spring you put the clock forward, in autumn back.

114163.q: Roughly how efficient are today's standard commercial solar panels?
114163.e: Common silicon panels turn around a fifth of the incoming light energy into electricity. The rest mainly becomes heat or is reflected.
114163.m: Solar panels use about a fifth of sunlight.

114164.q: What material are most solar cells made of?
114164.e: Silicon is obtained from quartz sand. It is the most important material for solar cells and also for computer chips.
114164.m: Most solar cells are made of silicon.

114165.q: Which unit is used to give the peak power of a solar installation?
114165.e: Kilowatt peak means the power under standard test conditions with strong sunshine. In everyday use the installation usually supplies less.
114165.m: The peak power of a solar installation is measured in kilowatt peak.

114166.q: Which device in a solar installation converts the panels' direct current into alternating current for the household grid?
114166.e: Solar cells supply direct current, but the power grid works with alternating current. The inverter adapts the current accordingly.
114166.m: The inverter turns direct current into alternating current.

114167.q: What is it called when a household directly uses the electricity from its own solar installation?
114167.e: Electricity you use yourself doesn't have to be bought expensively from the grid. So high self-consumption pays off, for example if the washing machine runs at midday.
114167.m: Solar electricity you use yourself is called self-consumption.

114168.q: Why do solar installations in the Alps produce more electricity in winter than in the Swiss Plateau?
a: They are often above the fog, and snow reflects light
The Sun shines there at night
It is warmer in the mountains
The days there are longer in winter
114168.e: In winter the Swiss Plateau often lies under a blanket of high fog, while it is sunny in the mountains. Snow also throws extra light onto the panels, and cold improves their efficiency.
114168.m: Alpine solar installations are especially valuable in winter.

114169.q: A solar installation has 10 kWp and produces around 1000 kWh per kWp a year. Roughly how much electricity does it produce per year?
114169.e: You work out 10 kWp times 1000 kWh per kWp. That makes 10,000 kWh a year.
114169.m: The yearly yield is the installation's power times the yield per kilowatt peak.

114170.q: What is the main difference between solar thermal and photovoltaics?
a: Solar thermal produces heat, photovoltaics electricity
Solar thermal only works at night
114170.e: Solar thermal installations use sunlight to warm a liquid, for example for hot water or heating. Photovoltaics, on the other hand, produces electric current.
114170.m: Solar thermal gives heat, photovoltaics gives electricity.

114171.q: What is the part on the roof called that captures the Sun's heat in solar thermal systems?
114171.e: A solar collector contains a dark absorber that turns radiation into heat. A liquid carries this heat into the house.
114171.m: Solar collectors capture the Sun's heat.

114172.q: What is the vacuum in an evacuated tube collector for?
114172.e: In a vacuum there is no air that could carry heat away. That is why evacuated tubes work well even in the cold.
114172.m: A vacuum insulates especially well against heat loss.

114173.q: Why is glycol added to the water in many solar collectors?
a: So that it doesn't freeze in winter
114173.e: Glycol lowers the freezing point of the liquid. So the pipes on the roof don't burst even in frost.
114173.m: Glycol protects solar collectors from frost.

114174.q: Why are the absorbers of solar collectors coloured dark?
a: Dark surfaces absorb the most light
So that they don't look dirty
114174.e: Dark surfaces absorb almost all the light and turn it into heat. Light-coloured surfaces would reflect a lot of light.
114174.m: Dark surfaces get warmest in the sun.

114175.q: Where is the water heated by the Sun stored in the house?
114175.e: A well-insulated hot water tank, often called a boiler in Switzerland, keeps the water warm for hours. So warm water is still available in the evening.
114175.m: A hot water tank stores the warm water.

114176.q: What is a power station called in which many mirrors focus sunlight onto the top of a tall tower?
114176.e: The mirrors concentrate the light so strongly that very high temperatures arise in the tower. This produces steam, which drives a turbine.
114176.m: In a solar tower power station, mirrors focus sunlight onto a tower.

114177.q: What is solar thermal energy most often used for in Swiss detached houses?
114177.e: In detached houses, solar collectors often cover a large part of the hot water needed. Some systems also help with the heating.
114177.m: Solar thermal energy mainly supplies hot water.

114178.q: Which form of the wind's energy does a wind turbine use?
114178.e: The moving air turns the rotor, and a generator turns this into electricity. In physics the energy of movement is called kinetic energy.
114178.m: Wind turbines turn kinetic energy into electricity.

114179.q: How many rotor blades do most modern wind turbines have?
114179.e: Three blades are a good compromise between output, smooth running and the amount of material. That is why almost all large turbines have three rotor blades.
114179.m: Modern wind turbines usually have three rotor blades.

114180.q: The power of the wind grows with the cube of the wind speed. How many times greater is it at double the wind speed?
114180.e: You work out 2 cubed, so 2 times 2 times 2. That makes 8. That is why windy sites are so important.
114180.m: Twice as much wind brings eight times as much power.

114181.q: Can a wind turbine use all the energy of the wind?
a: No, the wind must keep flowing behind the rotor
Yes, good turbines use all of it
Yes, but only in a storm
No, wind turbines use no wind energy at all
114181.e: If a wind turbine took all the energy from the wind, the air behind the rotor would stand still and no more wind would follow. So it can only use part of it, at most about 59 per cent.
114181.m: No wind turbine can use all the energy of the wind.

114182.q: On which Swiss Alpine pass did a wind farm with five turbines start operating in 2020?
114182.e: The Gotthard wind farm stands at around 2100 metres above sea level near the Gotthard Hospice. It is one of the highest wind farms in Europe.
114182.m: Wind turbines have been turning on the Gotthard Pass since 2020.

114183.q: Why are many wind farms built at sea (offshore)?
a: The wind there is stronger and steadier
114183.e: Over the open sea there are no hills or forests to slow the wind. So offshore turbines produce more electricity, but are more expensive to build.
114183.m: At sea the wind blows more strongly and steadily.

114184.q: Roughly how high is the hub of large modern wind turbines on land?
114184.e: Modern turbines often have hub heights of over 100 metres. Higher up, the wind blows more strongly and steadily than near the ground.
114184.m: The higher a wind turbine, the more wind it catches.

114185.q: What does a wind turbine do in a very strong storm?
a: It switches itself off for protection
It turns as fast as possible
114185.e: Above a certain wind speed, the blades are turned out of the wind and the rotor is stopped. This protects the turbine from damage.
114185.m: In a storm, wind turbines switch off.

114186.q: What is an important disadvantage of wind power?
a: It uses a lot of oil
114186.e: When there is no wind the turbines stand still; when it is windy they produce a lot of electricity. So storage and other power stations are needed to balance this out.
114186.m: Wind power varies with the weather.

114187.q: Apart from methane, which gas is the second largest part of biogas?
114187.e: As well as methane, biogas contains a lot of carbon dioxide, which does not burn. It is removed before the gas is fed into the gas network.
114187.m: As well as methane, biogas contains a lot of carbon dioxide.

114188.q: Under what condition do bacteria break down the material in a biogas plant?
114188.e: In the airtight digester, bacteria break down the material without oxygen. This produces the flammable gas.
114188.m: Biogas forms when bacteria work without oxygen.

114189.q: Which materials are often fermented in farm biogas plants?
114189.e: Slurry, manure, green waste and food leftovers contain a lot of organic material. Bacteria can make biogas from it.
114189.m: Biogas can be made from slurry and green waste.

114190.q: What is done with the digestate left over in a biogas plant?
a: It is burnt with the rubbish
It is thrown into the lake
It is used to build roads
114190.e: The digestate still contains many nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus. So it is spread on the fields.
114190.m: Digestate from biogas plants is a good fertiliser.

114191.q: Which installation produces electricity and heat at the same time from biogas?
a: A combined heat and power plant
114191.e: In a combined heat and power plant, a gas engine drives a generator. The waste heat from the engine is used for heating.
114191.m: A combined heat and power plant supplies electricity and heat at the same time.

114192.q: What is the gas called that forms in sewage works when sewage sludge is treated?
114192.e: In the digestion towers of sewage works, bacteria break down the sludge without oxygen. The sewage gas produced is usually used right there for electricity and heat.
114192.m: Sewage works produce sewage gas from sludge.

114193.q: On average, how much does the temperature in the Earth's crust rise for every 100 metres of depth?
114193.e: This rise is called the geothermal gradient. On average it is about 3 degrees per 100 metres, but it can vary from place to place.
114193.m: For every 100 metres of depth it gets about 3 degrees warmer.

114194.q: At the surface it is 10 °C, and it gets 3 °C warmer every 100 metres. Roughly how warm is it at a depth of 3000 metres?
114194.e: 3000 metres is 30 times 100 metres, so 30 times 3 °C, which is 90 °C. Add the 10 °C at the surface, making 100 °C in total.
114194.m: Deep underground the rock is very hot.

114195.q: Which device is used together with a ground source probe to heat a house?
114195.e: The ground probe takes heat of around 10 degrees from the ground. The heat pump raises this heat to a higher temperature for heating.
114195.m: A heat pump makes ground heat usable for heating.

114196.q: A heat pump produces 4 kWh of heat from 1 kWh of electricity. How many kWh of this come from the surroundings?
114196.e: Of the 4 kWh of heat, 1 kWh comes from the electricity. The remaining 4 minus 1, so 3 kWh, the heat pump takes from the ground, air or water.
114196.m: A heat pump takes most of its heat from the surroundings.

114197.q: In which Swiss city was a deep geothermal project stopped in 2006 because it caused noticeable earthquakes?
114197.e: In the “Deep Heat Mining” project in Basel, water was pressed into the rock at great depth. This caused several noticeable earthquakes, after which the project was stopped.
114197.m: Deep geothermal energy can cause earthquakes.

114198.q: Where does a large part of the heat inside the Earth come from?
a: From the decay of radioactive substances
From the friction of the wind
114198.e: Inside the Earth, elements such as uranium, thorium and potassium decay and release heat. There is also leftover heat from the time the Earth was formed.
114198.m: Radioactive decay heats the inside of the Earth.

114199.q: Which island country covers a large part of its heat and electricity needs with geothermal energy?
114199.e: Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge with many volcanoes. Almost all homes there are heated with geothermal heat.
114199.m: Iceland heats almost entirely with geothermal energy.

114200.q: What is an advantage of geothermal energy over solar energy?
a: It is available day and night
It can only be used by the sea
114200.e: The heat inside the Earth is always there, whatever the weather or time of day. Solar cells, on the other hand, only produce electricity when there is light.
114200.m: Geothermal energy is available round the clock.

114201.e: Wood chips are pieces of wood a few centimetres in size. They are made when branches and leftover wood are chopped up in a chipper.
114201.m: Wood chips are small chopped pieces of wood.

114202.q: Why is heating with wood from sustainable forestry considered largely CO2-neutral?
a: The tree took in as much CO2 while growing
Wood contains no carbon at all
114202.e: Burning releases only as much CO2 as the tree took from the air before. The condition is that the same amount of forest grows back.
114202.m: When burnt, wood releases the CO2 that the tree took in.

114203.q: Why do dry wood chips give more usable heat than wet ones?
a: With wet wood, energy is lost evaporating the water
114203.e: The water in the wood has to be evaporated first, which takes a lot of energy. Wet wood also burns less well and produces more smoke.
114203.m: Dry wood heats better than wet wood.

114204.q: What is a system called in which a central wood chip heating plant supplies many buildings with heat through pipes?
114204.e: In a district heating network, hot water flows through insulated pipes to the connected houses. In many Swiss municipalities a single large wood-fired plant heats a whole neighbourhood this way.
114204.m: A district heating network brings heat from one central plant to many houses.

114205.q: Which pollutant is a particular problem with wood heating and is held back with filters?
114205.e: Burning wood produces tiny dust particles that get into the lungs. Larger plants therefore have electrostatic or fabric filters.
114205.m: Wood heating needs good filters against fine dust.

114206.q: Roughly what share of Switzerland's area is covered by forest?
114206.e: Around 32 per cent of Switzerland is forested. Among other things, this forest supplies energy wood for wood chip heating.
114206.m: About a third of Switzerland is forest.

114207.q: Where does the wood for wood chip heating usually come from?
a: From leftover wood from forest care and sawmills
114207.e: For wood chips, mainly branches, thin trunks and waste from sawmills are used. This makes use of wood that would otherwise hardly be needed.
114207.m: Wood chips are mostly made from leftover wood.

114208.q: In an automatic system, how do the wood chips get from the store into the boiler?
114208.e: A turning screw conveyor pushes the chips from the silo to the combustion chamber. So the heating runs without manual work.
114208.m: A screw conveyor brings the chips into the boiler.

114209.q: What are the two main aims of the Energy Strategy 2050?
a: Using energy more efficiently and expanding renewable energy
Importing more oil and mining coal
Building new nuclear power stations and more gas heating
Less hydropower and more diesel generators
114209.e: The Energy Strategy 2050 aims to lower energy use and increase efficiency. At the same time, hydropower and new renewable energy such as solar and wind are to be expanded.
114209.m: Efficiency and renewable energy are the pillars of the Energy Strategy 2050.

114210.q: According to the Energy Strategy 2050, what applies to new nuclear power stations in Switzerland?
a: No new ones may be approved
They are specially supported by the Confederation
114210.e: The Energy Act forbids general licences for new nuclear power stations. The existing ones may keep running as long as they are safe.
114210.m: New nuclear power stations may not be approved in Switzerland.

114211.q: Which event in 2011 triggered the Energy Strategy 2050?
a: The opening of the Gotthard Base Tunnel
The Football World Cup in Switzerland
114211.e: After the serious accident at the Japanese nuclear power station in Fukushima, the Federal Council and Parliament decided in 2011 on a new direction for Swiss energy policy.
114211.m: Fukushima led to Switzerland's nuclear phase-out.

114212.q: Which nuclear power station was the first in Switzerland to be shut down for good, at the end of 2019?
114212.e: The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern went off the grid on 20 December 2019. Since then it has been dismantled.
114212.m: Mühleberg has been shut down since 2019.

114213.q: What is the Electricity Act, which Switzerland approved in June 2024, meant to promote?
a: More electricity from coal-fired power stations
The building of new nuclear power stations
114213.e: The Electricity Act was approved with around 69 per cent voting yes. It is meant to speed up the expansion of solar, wind and hydropower.
114213.m: In 2024 Switzerland clearly said yes to more renewable electricity.

114214.q: What climate target for 2050 did Switzerland set itself with the Climate and Innovation Act of 2023?
114214.e: The act was approved by the people on 18 June 2023. By 2050, only as much greenhouse gas is to be emitted as can be absorbed again.
114214.m: Switzerland aims to reach net zero by 2050.

114215.q: What is the label for Swiss municipalities with a model energy policy called?
114215.e: The Energy City label honours municipalities that, for example, promote renewable energy and save energy. It is supported by the federal SwissEnergy programme.
114215.m: Energy Cities work especially hard for a sustainable energy policy.

114216.q: Which type of rechargeable battery is most often used today in home storage systems and electric cars?
114216.e: Lithium-ion batteries store a lot of energy for little weight. That is why they are in phones, laptops, electric cars and home storage systems.
114216.m: Modern storage mostly uses lithium-ion batteries.

114217.q: In which unit do you give how much energy a battery storage system can hold?
114217.e: The kilowatt hour is a unit of energy. The power in kilowatts, on the other hand, tells you how quickly a storage system can release energy.
114217.m: The amount a battery can store is measured in kilowatt hours.

114218.q: A home battery holds 10 kWh. How long can it supply a 500-watt device?
114218.e: 500 watts is 0.5 kW. You work out 10 kWh divided by 0.5 kW, which makes 20 hours.
114218.m: Running time is stored energy divided by power.

114219.q: Because of what it does, what is the Nant de Drance pumped storage power station in Valais often called?
114219.e: When there is surplus electricity, Nant de Drance pumps water into an upper lake and lets it flow back through turbines when needed. So it stores electricity like a gigantic battery.
114219.m: Pumped storage power stations store electricity as water pumped uphill.

114220.q: For which invention did John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019?
114220.e: From the 1970s the three scientists developed the basis of the rechargeable lithium-ion battery. It made portable electronics and electric cars possible.
114220.m: The lithium-ion battery was honoured with the Nobel Prize in 2019.

114221.q: In what form is the energy stored in a charged rechargeable battery?
114221.e: When charging, chemical reactions take place in the battery that are reversed when it discharges. The chemical energy then becomes electrical energy again.
114221.m: A rechargeable battery stores electricity as chemical energy.

114222.q: Why do old rechargeable batteries belong at the collection point and not in the rubbish?
a: They contain valuable and harmful substances
They are too heavy for the bin bag
114222.e: Batteries contain metals such as lithium or cobalt that can be recycled. They can also catch fire or pollute the environment.
114222.m: Old batteries go to the collection point.

114223.q: What happens to a rechargeable battery's capacity after many charging cycles?
a: It stays the same for ever
114223.e: With every charge and discharge the battery ages a little. After many years it can therefore store less energy than at the start.
114223.m: Rechargeable batteries lose capacity over time.

114224.q: What is the distance an electric car can drive on one full battery charge called?
114224.e: The range depends on battery size, driving style and temperature. In winter it is usually shorter, because the cold weakens the battery and the heating uses electricity.
114224.m: Range tells you how far an electric car can go on one charge.

114225.q: What is it called when an electric car feeds energy back into the battery while braking?
114225.e: When braking, the electric motor works as a generator and charges the battery. So less energy is lost as heat in the brakes.
114225.m: Through regenerative braking an electric car recovers braking energy.

114226.q: An electric car uses 18 kWh per 100 km. How much energy does it need for 250 km?
114226.e: 250 km is 2.5 times 100 km. You work out 18 kWh times 2.5, which makes 45 kWh.
114226.m: You work out the energy needed from consumption times distance.

114227.q: A battery charge needs 20 kWh, and one kilowatt hour costs 30 centimes. What does the charge cost?
114227.e: You work out 20 times 30 centimes, which is 600 centimes. 600 centimes are 6 francs.
114227.m: Electricity cost is the amount of energy times the price per kilowatt hour.

114228.q: What drive did the first car to go faster than 100 km/h, in 1899, have?
114228.e: In 1899 the racing car “La Jamais Contente” drove electrically at over 105 km/h. So electric cars already existed more than a hundred years ago.
114228.m: The first car to go over 100 km/h was electric.

114229.q: With which type of current do rapid charging stations charge an electric car's battery directly?
a: With three-phase current from the socket
114229.e: Batteries can only store direct current. Rapid charging stations convert the mains current inside the charger itself and charge directly at high power.
114229.m: Rapid charging stations charge with direct current.

114230.q: Which part of a petrol car is missing on a purely electric car?
114230.e: An electric car burns no fuel and so gives off no exhaust gases while driving. So it doesn't need an exhaust pipe.
114230.m: Electric cars drive without exhaust gases from an exhaust pipe.

114231.q: Where should the electricity come from for an electric car to be as climate-friendly as possible?
114231.e: An electric car is only as clean as the electricity it is charged with. With electricity from water, sun or wind, its CO2 emissions are especially low.
114231.m: Electric cars are most climate-friendly with green electricity.

114232.q: Which process uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen?
114232.e: In electrolysis, current flows through water. Hydrogen forms at one electrode and oxygen at the other.

114233.q: Which device produces electric current directly from hydrogen and oxygen?
114233.e: In a fuel cell the two gases react with each other in a controlled way. This produces electricity, and the only waste left is water.
114233.m: A fuel cell turns hydrogen into electricity.

114234.q: What is hydrogen called that is produced with electricity from renewable energy?
114234.e: If electricity from water, sun or wind is used to produce it, hardly any CO2 is created. It is then called green hydrogen.
114234.m: Green hydrogen is produced with renewable electricity.

114235.q: From which raw material is most hydrogen today, so-called grey hydrogen, produced?
114235.e: Most hydrogen today is obtained from natural gas. This produces a lot of CO2, so it is not considered climate-friendly.
114235.m: Grey hydrogen comes from natural gas.

114236.q: What special property does hydrogen have in the periodic table?
114236.e: Hydrogen has the atomic number 1 and consists of just one proton and one electron. It is the lightest and most common element in the universe.

114237.q: Why is hydrogen squeezed very hard in car tanks?
a: Because it is very light and would otherwise take up too much space
Because it would otherwise not burn
Because it would otherwise become poisonous
114237.e: Hydrogen is the lightest gas. So that enough of it fits in a tank, it is compressed at very high pressure.
114237.m: For cars, hydrogen is stored at very high pressure.

114238.q: What is an explosive mixture of hydrogen and oxygen called?
114238.e: When ignited, hydrogen and oxygen react with a loud bang to form water. That is why handling hydrogen needs strict safety rules.
114238.m: Oxyhydrogen is an explosive mixture of hydrogen and oxygen.

114239.q: What disadvantage does hydrogen have as an energy store compared with a rechargeable battery?
a: A lot of energy is lost making it and turning it back into electricity
It cannot be stored at all
It only gives heat and never electricity
114239.e: Going from electricity via hydrogen back to electricity, often only around a third of the energy is left. A battery loses much less.
114239.m: The detour via hydrogen costs a lot of energy.

114240.q: Which two Swiss pilots flew around the world in the solar aircraft Solar Impulse 2?
114240.e: Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg took turns at the controls on the individual legs. The journey lasted from 2015 to 2016.
114240.m: Piccard and Borschberg flew around the world on solar power.

114241.q: In which year did Solar Impulse 2 complete the first round-the-world flight by a solar aircraft?
114241.e: On 26 July 2016 Solar Impulse 2 landed back in Abu Dhabi. It was the first round-the-world flight by an aircraft using only solar energy.
114241.m: In 2016 a solar aircraft flew around the world for the first time.

114242.q: In which city did Solar Impulse 2 start and finish its flight around the world?
114242.e: It took off in March 2015 in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates. The plane also landed there again after about 40,000 kilometres.
114242.m: The Solar Impulse round-the-world trip began and ended in Abu Dhabi.

114243.q: Roughly how big was the wingspan of Solar Impulse 2?
114243.e: With a wingspan of about 72 metres, Solar Impulse 2 was wider than a jumbo jet. The wings had room for thousands of solar cells.
114243.m: Solar Impulse 2 had bigger wings than a jumbo jet.

114244.q: Where were most of the solar cells on Solar Impulse 2?
114244.e: The huge wings offered the largest surface for thousands of solar cells. More cells were on the body and the tail.
114244.m: The solar cells of Solar Impulse were mainly on the wings.

114245.q: How was Solar Impulse 2 able to keep flying at night?
a: With power from batteries charged during the day
With a spare tank full of kerosene
With moonlight on the solar cells
114245.e: During the day the solar cells produced more electricity than needed and charged the batteries. At night the batteries drove the propellers.
114245.m: Batteries stored solar power for the night.

114246.q: Roughly how long did the longest leg of Solar Impulse 2, from Japan to Hawaii, take?
114246.e: In 2015 André Borschberg flew from Nagoya to Hawaii in about 118 hours without stopping. That was a record for the longest solo flight.
114246.m: A Solar Impulse pilot flew for almost five days without landing.

114247.q: How many people could fit in the cockpit of Solar Impulse 2?
114247.e: The cockpit was only about 3.8 cubic metres and built for a single pilot. He had to fly alone for days and slept only in short naps.

114248.q: Why does carbon dioxide (CO2) contribute to the warming of the Earth?
a: It holds back heat radiation in the atmosphere
114248.e: CO2 is a greenhouse gas. It lets sunlight through but holds back part of the heat radiated by the Earth.
114248.m: CO2 acts like a greenhouse in the atmosphere.

114249.q: Roughly how much CO2 is produced when one litre of petrol is burned?
114249.e: When it burns, the carbon in the petrol combines with oxygen from the air. That is why the CO2 produced is heavier than the petrol itself.
114249.m: One litre of petrol produces more than two kilograms of CO2.

114250.q: A car uses 5 litres of petrol on a journey. Each litre produces 2.3 kg of CO2. How much CO2 does it give off?
114250.e: You work out 5 times 2.3 kg. That gives 11.5 kg of CO2.
114250.m: CO2 emissions grow with every litre burned.

114251.q: Which sector causes the largest share of Switzerland's domestic greenhouse gas emissions (as of 2023)?
114251.e: Transport, above all cars and lorries running on petrol and diesel, is the biggest source. Buildings and industry come next.
114251.m: In Switzerland, transport gives off the most greenhouse gases.

114252.q: On which energy sources has Switzerland charged a CO2 levy since 2008?
a: On fuels such as heating oil and natural gas
114252.e: The CO2 levy makes fossil fuels more expensive and is meant to encourage saving. A large part is paid back to the population through health insurance premiums.
114252.m: In Switzerland, heating oil and natural gas carry a CO2 levy.

114253.q: How has the amount of CO2 in the air changed since the start of industrialisation?
a: It only changes between day and night
114253.e: Before about 1750 the air contained about 280 ppm of CO2; today it is over 420 ppm (as of 2024). The main reason is the burning of coal, oil and gas.
114253.m: Since industrialisation, the CO2 content of the air has risen sharply.

114254.q: In the 2015 Paris climate agreement, to what limit do countries want to keep global warming if possible?
114254.e: Warming should stay well below 2 °C compared with pre-industrial times, ideally at 1.5 °C. For that, CO2 emissions must fall sharply.
114254.m: The Paris Agreement aims for no more than 1.5 degrees of warming.

114255.q: What do you call a natural system, such as a growing forest, that takes in more CO2 than it releases?
114255.e: A sink removes more CO2 from the atmosphere than it releases. Besides forests, bogs and oceans are also important sinks.
114255.m: Forests, bogs and seas are important carbon sinks.

114256.q: What is the total of all greenhouse gases caused by a person or a product called?
114256.e: The carbon footprint adds up all emissions, for example from heating, travel, food and shopping. This lets you compare different lifestyles.
114256.m: Your carbon footprint shows how much greenhouse gas you cause.

a: A vertical cut through the soil
A map showing all soil types
A device for measuring soil moisture
The top layer of leaves in a wood
114257.e: A soil profile is a vertical cut through the soil from the surface down to the rock. In it you can see the different layers on top of each other.
114257.m: A soil profile shows the soil in a vertical cut.

114258.q: What is the best way to look at a soil profile?
114258.e: For a soil profile you dig a profile pit with a vertical wall. On this wall you can see the layers of the soil.
114258.m: In a profile pit you can see the layers of the soil.

114259.q: What does a soil profile consist of?
a: Layers lying on top of each other
114259.e: A soil profile is divided into several layers that differ in colour, grain size and humus content. You can see them well on the wall of a pit.
114259.m: A soil profile consists of several layers.

114260.q: What lies at the very bottom of a typical soil profile?
114260.e: At the very bottom lies the rock from which the soil formed through weathering. Above it come the subsoil and topsoil.
114260.m: Beneath the soil lies the rock it formed from.

114261.q: What lies at the very top of a woodland soil profile?
a: A layer of leaves and needles
114261.e: At the very top in a wood lies the litter layer of fallen leaves, needles and twigs. It is gradually broken down by soil organisms.
114261.m: In a wood, a litter layer of leaves covers the soil.

114262.q: What does a very dark layer in a soil profile usually indicate?
114262.e: Humus colours the soil dark brown to black. The more humus a layer contains, the darker it usually is.
114262.m: Dark soil usually contains lots of humus.

114263.q: Which tool do you use to take a soil sample from deep down without digging a pit?
114263.e: A soil auger is a metal rod with a groove that you hammer into the ground. When you pull it out, you see a narrow strip of the soil profile.
114263.m: With a soil auger you can examine soil without a pit.
